en: The First Chapter: The Refutation of Udayana. Om, homage to Tārā.
Having understood that the path of one's own words is most delightful and remains as the legacy of the virtuous,
I shall, on the basis of Udayana’s statement, speak of the path of the destruction of one's own words and conduct.
Indeed, here [is the place] resembling a massive pillar situated upon the girdle of the vast mountain range.

The opponent's [objection], which was raised from the suspicion that the capacity or incapacity expressed by the venerable Jñānaśrīmitra’s words [in the *Jñānasārasamuccaya*] had not been fully clarified, is now rendered futile once the distinction [between the two types of existence] is established through the conjunction of the contradictory properties of capacity and incapacity; thus,
the opponent's attempt to attach [the property of] "existence" (*sattva*) and so forth [to the subject] is frustrated.
For indeed, by means of a complete and unimpaired protective covering,

the seeds of the adversaries— whose presence is established through the full convergence of conditions consisting of the direct contact of earth, water, and air— grow, developing through a transformation made delightful by qualities such as self-dependent growth arising therefrom.

The sprouts are manifested as being produced from conditions that exist in each respective instance. Their status as conditions characterized as previously described is established through the following: the excellence residing in their individual foundations, the possibility of direct perception and non-perception of the subsequent state, and the conceptualization of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). One must establish the correspondence of this with the specific totality of auxiliary factors (*sahakāri-sākalya*) nurtured by that [conception]; otherwise, if it were dependent upon the proximity of other conditions, there would be a sequence [of production], just as in the case of a seed.

The excellence of its specific temporal sequence (*kṣaṇaviśeṣasauṣṭhava*) would burst open the adjunct (*upādhi*), such that one could ascertain whether germination occurs by determining whether the subsequent moment remains present or not in its state of having or lacking the totality of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri*).
Thus, because the moment coiled within the interior of the granary is distinct [from the next],
the wheel of detailed investigation proceeds to analyze whether the cluster of seeds, whose body has spread across the field through the succession of auxiliary moments, is a single entity or many.

Furthermore, they do not state this in a straightforward manner; rather, having introduced the notion of another distinct nature that is deluded by the proximity of causal conditions accompanied by auxiliary factors, they—
with hearts softened by the desire to grasp their own position and its counter-position— proclaim "this is the proof" when there is a contradiction with the means of valid cognition.

In order to establish the capacity for the desire to grasp [an object] and so forth, one directly engages in practical activity by saying "at that time it does that" or "it certainly does that. Furthermore, just as there is a longing for the realization of freedom from doubt regarding the truth of the means as they have been revealed— wherein the body is prostrated with excellence— and just as the category of momentariness (*kṣaṇatva*) is established even when isolated,

yet even though it is thus isolated, it is perceived as "it acts" or "it certainly acts"— this very consequence (*prasaṅga*), by way of its own consequence, illuminates the difference in substrata between acting and not acting as they meet in prior and subsequent times.
For instance: (4) at the conclusion, the capacity to produce the intended effect is examined by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and found to reside in each [constituent] individually.

By means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the totality [of causes] such as the earth, the potter’s workshop, and so forth, is loosened; and having observed that the qualifier is pervaded by its own particularity through the process of the destruction of the prior and posterior states, it is inferred—being free from the distinction [between itself and others]—as being concealed by the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyoga-vyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*).
For a universal (*sāmānya*) would otherwise be devoid of particulars. (6)
Like a hare's horn;
agency without qualification would be equal to the son of a barren woman.

Therefore, because our own mental representations do not appear as the actual state of things, how could there be such [identity] for entities? In that regard, O Venerable Ones, the extreme similarity between the prior and the subsequent within a single continuum—[a state where] there is barrenness [of difference] and a lack of agency—is to be experienced through the analogy of hair, locks of hair, a lotus, and a stalk, just like the perception of a sound.

Let it be shown that the distinctions produced by the differences in their respective accompaniments, such as heat and so forth, are merely apparent; for recognition, which perceives identity between prior and posterior states, bears the supreme essence of all trustworthiness regarding ultimate reality.
Regarding the phrase "leading to confusion":
the reason for favoring one side and refuting the other is that the very nature of the reason (hetu) is corrupted by the proponent (*bhavya*).

For instance, its agency toward others is like that of a neutral party, because it acts with delay as agreed upon by both the proponent and the opponent; thus, it is devoid of the establishment of specific distinctions such as being a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and so forth.

Furthermore, by the power of skillful composition, even for those who partake of both stages and whose activity consists of speaking about what has already come to be, the nature of agency—which is being cultivated—is in reality that which brings about the exclusion of absolute non-connection;
and as for the nature of agency being cultivated, is it in reality that which brings about the exclusion of absolute non-connection? [This] is the ground of the delusion of the breath.
Even though the determination of the actual experience is unstable, it is nevertheless accepted by the venerable one— or by another— in whatever manner is appropriate;
that is to say, the nature of the agent as being "excluded from non-connection" (ayogavyavacchinna-kartṛtva) must be proclaimed.

Even though the established order of experience and so forth has vanished, those who consider themselves self-composed are nonetheless imprisoned by the necessity of accepting one or the other of the two positions propounded by the assembly of venerable masters and the like. Since both [positions] are grasped through the implication of the meaning (*arthagṛhīta*) and are thus adorned with the gateway of the Dvāpara age, tell me, which one here falls into a state of being without refuge? If it is asked, "What is the distinction between these faults?
it is said: this very point is the crux—namely, that whenever...

Whatever is the locus for the establishment of its capacity, that indeed performs that [action] at that time; just as in the state of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), even when a fraction of time is deficient, the distinction between entities is demonstrated by taking up the limits of the golden effect, based on the locus where capacity is established even if previously unmentioned. This is how the logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) is to be characterized in the position that agency excludes non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*). And yet, it is never perceived as being devoid of its concomitants (*niḥsahacara*).

The wheel of the letter *ha* (*hakāricakra*) proceeds to establish that the intended entity is the agent through the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*), such that it must be accepted as its own effect; and here, the opposite [view] is to be rejected. Nevertheless, this might appear like a painting on a wall-less surface when the state of being non-exclusive (*anekānta*) has arisen. For even if there is fitness for the conventional usage of capacity, what kind of establishment of the power set in motion by agency is there to be refuted in a *prasaṅga* proof? (p. 5)
This is because it aims to establish the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that proves its very nature as being non-delayed;
for it is impossible to attribute the characteristic of delayed action—defined by the fact that "it acts only when all auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are present"—to its state as a solitary entity.

Furthermore, if one proclaims its agency as having such an intrinsic nature that "it necessarily acts when all auxiliary causes are present," then the lack of fame [of its agency] is precisely due to the delay already accomplished.

Because this position is consistent with the words of the Elders (*sthavira*) and because it is sound, alas, the darkness of delusion of others has not been dispelled even by the exceedingly pure sunbeams of well-spoken verses.

For, by thus introducing the qualification of the seed’s agency as being entirely dependent upon auxiliary conditions, the opposing position is agitated; and even "non-delayed agency," which is a specific form of that [agency] established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is properly refuted when one follows [the logic]. This is because non-delayed agency is the very nature of the general property of agency in its final state, as established through perception and non-perception.

Having conceived of [the agent] as pervasive due to the diversity of its individual manifestations, and since no other mode is perceived, you accept that the general property of agency (*kartṛtvasāmānya*) undergoes transformation into the form of non-delayed causal efficacy (*anakṣepakartṛtva*). However, this does not coherently serve as a relevant factor in the context of the *prasaṅga* (reductio).

For instance, although the agency of a seed is observed even in the presence of auxiliary causes, it is not to be qualified by that very association; otherwise, even a fragment of stone would possess such agency. Rather, it belongs to the [seed] alone.

Or rather, because the individuality of the seed is established through the understanding of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), since the collection [of conditions] is excluded from the category of stones;
and this individuality does not constitute a distinct agency for the seed.

How could a contact with the circle of auxiliary causes—which is by nature the absence of the seed's individuality and thus lacks individual form—be able to produce a distinction? For it is not accepted by the learned that "the eye does not exist, and yet it is distinguished by that [absence]."

Precisely because it does not produce conceptualization without a cause, an entity such as a fragment of stone is not taken up by one who seeks an effect; for what specific purpose would it need to be employed? However, this is when such a qualification has been removed.

Now, at that time, regarding the remaining husk of the rice grain which has been determined to be the cause—[the opponent might argue] that it could perhaps act alone during the moment of the assembly of the causal complex, as this would not be ruled out by the inference of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*). This is the first undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) mixed with the [opponent's] position, and this is the fault sought [by us].
That is incorrect— for is capacity (sāmarthya) indeed action (kṛti) or fitness (yogyatā)?
Not the first, because it would entail the consequence of being indistinguishable from the probandum (sādhya).
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; for that [capacity] would be either the totality of auxiliary conditions or the individual capacity itself.
It cannot be the first, because it would result in proving what is already established.

Furthermore, there is the non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*) due to the opponent’s lack of admission [of the subject]. For who indeed does not admit that "whatever possesses the convergence of auxiliary causes necessarily performs [the action]"—it is precisely such a person whom one would address when proving [this]? Moreover, we do not admit that [the entity] possesses the convergence of auxiliary causes at the time it is not performing [the action].
For a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) would proceed from this [general capacity].
However, specific capacity must be either seedhood as established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), or a specific sub-classification within that,
or else the state of being characterized by the absence of an effect due to the deficiency of auxiliary causes (sahakārin).
Not the first, because even that which does not produce [the effect] is established by perception as being of the same class as the seed;
for you, too, have no disagreement on this point. Nor the other, because since I do not admit that [the seed] produces [the effect], the example would be deficient in the probans (*sādhanavikala*).
For what person of sound mind would indeed accept that which is devoid of any means of valid cognition?
For it is not perceived through direct perception, since there is no such determination [of it].
Nor can it be established by inference, because there is no indicative mark (*liṅga*).
If there were no distinction whatsoever, how then could there be acting and non-acting? (9)
Who says "no"?

Following the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that determines whether [the nature] consists in a difference of genus or in the presence or absence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), we do not perceive such a determiner.
Nevertheless, if this entity—which, while situated in the midst of its auxiliaries, has the nature of producing an effect without delay—existed previously as well; [then...]

If it is argued that one who acts forcibly at that time cannot be thwarted even by a hundred curses from the gods, this may be correct provided that the nature of an entity as necessarily producing its effect falls within the scope of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). But how is that established? We do not know. If it is argued that it is established through *reductio ad absurdum* (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*tadviparyaya*), we say no.
Because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*):

for the establishment of their having such an intrinsic nature (*svabhāvatva*) depends upon their activity, and the establishment of their having such an intrinsic nature depends upon that activity. [Objection:

It might be argued that in this matter, the very production of the effect is the proof (*pramāṇa*) regarding the persistence of an intrinsic nature that acts with delay; for if there were no such persistence, the effect would never arise at all.
No, for if that which has the nature of acting with delay were never to act at all, its very essence would be contradicted.
Therefore, the meaning of "acting with delay" is that it does not act as long as the collection of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) is not present.
And thus, while it is impossible to prove [this] regarding the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces an effect, it is not so regarding the difference in their intrinsic natures (*jātibheda*).

For in this regard, do those [causes], being mutually dependent according to experience, produce the effect by being proximate to one another due to their nature of acting with delay; or rather, as imagined otherwise, do they possess a nature of acting swiftly? It is on this point [that the doubt lies].
The production of the effect would thus be entirely non-vigilant.

Nor is the third [alternative] possible, because of contradiction: it is a contradiction to claim that something both lacks an effect due to the absence of auxiliary causes and yet possesses the effect in the absence of those auxiliaries.

(7) Therefore, if it were the case that whatever a thing does not produce due to its very absence, it produces that [effect] due to its presence, then this would be the supreme and entire essence of the proof of stability. By this, the argument that "the state of being within the scope of the conventional usage of 'capacity' is the logical reason" is refuted;
for we observe even a seed—which is within the scope of such usage—not producing a sprout.
If it is argued that this is not the primary conventional usage there because it has birth as its cause,
and because otherwise an undesirable restriction [of change] would follow— [we reply: no.
Furthermore, what kind of birth (*janman*) serves as the cause for the primary conventional usage of "capacity"?
It cannot be the cause consisting in the act of projection (*ākṣepa*), because that is unestablished.

Furthermore, since a restriction (*niyama*) functions as a cause only when there is a completeness of auxiliary factors such as the *sahakārin*, it arises by virtue of having such an inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
Consequently, this conventional usage pertains solely to the occasion of production, and not to the establishment of a pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Thus, he who is rich in extreme intellectual acuity, capable of exposing the exceedingly harsh and formidable mass [of arguments] that resembles the shell of a mature tortoise’s back...

What more need be said here regarding this one whose fame proclaims him as the drummer for the dancing girl of the city of the three worlds, as he dances with joy because his [the world's] suffering has been torn asunder?
By this, agency is established through the exclusion of non-connection. (3)

Setting aside even the transformation into a general state of agency, the desperate attempt by the rogue to appropriate [the opponent's position] has begun as follows: "Whenever and whatever thing possesses the capacity for a causal operation, it necessarily performs that very action at that time;
just as a seed, even in its prior distinct state, is determined to be of such a nature that it is not defeated by non-seedhood and is swift in its efficacy, so too is this [agent]."

And one should not conclude that it simply does not act; rather, a skillful person should reach such a conclusion through an internal reflection that thoroughly examines the opposite of that [position].

Thus, the seed which has undergone the transformation of its non-seed state is determined to possess agency—arising from its general nature as an agent established through the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) resulting from the undertaking of the perception and non-perception of phenomena—which implies the implication of what was previously unimplied.

The proof (*sādhana*) here is the capacity for the conventional usage of "capable," which is produced by that which is characterized as "acting" or "not acting non-delayedly" (*anakṣepakāritva*); and the probandum (*sādhya*) is the duality of agency—namely, "it acts" or "it necessarily acts"—occurring in succession, just as it is accepted by the opponent.
This is possible because, by rejecting both positions, a general characteristic (*sāmānya*) exists that is not pervaded by its specific instances (*viśeṣa*).

Even by means of the two positions (*pakṣa*), the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*tadviparyaya*) must likewise be characterized. For even for a single moment, there is no room for a multitude of refutations against that which lacks the causal capacity for the conventional activity of performing [an action]. Whatever is perceived as lacking the capacity to perform [an action] is devoid of that performance; just as a seed in its final state—or even in a prior distinct state—is considered not to have produced sprout-ness.

Thus, by means of a mind made smooth through a single unifying reflection, the wise have never determined that each individual [cause] possesses the capacity for production— even though such a conclusion is traditionally taught— when it is being gathered together, because at the time of its placement within the difficult-to-traverse interior of the causal mechanism, the entire range of directions is traversed by the discourse of living beings.
Therefore, there is no satisfaction in accepting each [of these] individually—that the perfection of the wise consists in their own awakening and their composure;

that self-nature is the state of being the counter-correlate of non-existence; that it is "at that very time" (tadaiva); that it is "in that very place" (tatraiva); that it is "accompanied by both"; and that it is "attached in that same way"—all of which have their grandiosity shattered by the staff of one's own [logical] category, and even the concealment of one's own words has been reduced to a mere flight. Thus, this calamity is a total uprooting; how is it to be remedied?

"Even by a thousand streams of tears shed by the clouds, there is no protection for this wretched one who cries out in distress and terror until the end of his life"—thus, even with a compassionate heart, he does not cross over [the suffering] through speech in the method of debate. Enough with these manifold, false fabrications of poetic fancy; O worthy one, though you are capable, be intent upon the principles of logic (*nyāya*).
For instance, what is this "logic" of yours? Or, even by this much, what intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity is established?

If it is argued that there is no category other than the proponent's position (*pakṣa*) and the opponent's counter-position (*vipakṣa*), we say no; for at the time of stating a refutation, since the inconclusive unestablished reason (*sandigdhāsiddhi*) is established simply by the absence of certainty, the preliminary stage of the debate reaches its conclusion through this means. Furthermore, a *prasaṅga* argument is introduced because there is no other possible mode [of proof], whether by way of the opponent’s own admission or by way of what is merely conceivable.

If you argue that, having stated the fault of being "doubtfully unestablished" (*sandigdhāsiddhatva*), I myself do not actually accept that as a refutation, then let this be considered: you indeed admit agency (*kartṛtva*), and since you rely on recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), that agency remains exactly as it was previously. Thus, the substratum—which is of the nature of a seed—results in an uninterrupted state of agency defined by the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavacchedana*). How can such an indestructible [position] be withered by the fault of being doubtfully unestablished?
Regarding its capacity for projection (*ākṣepakāritva*), it is also said that the portion presided over therein—

having been cultivated as a portion presided over by [the agent] through the manifestation of the totality within the womb— is then spoken of as existing in reality as something inseparable from the portion thus presided over;
for that very seed existed even previously.

How can the *prasaṅgasādhana*—which establishes that [the cause] possesses the fitness for the conventional usage of "capacity" produced by the generation of the moment that brings about non-delayed action—be shaken off on the grounds of being "doubtfully unestablished" (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*)? For there is no prior stage of the debate consisting of the expansion of the opponent's position (*uttarapakṣa*), which relies upon the adversary, if one does not accept the collapse of its own nature; thus it is like a *prasaṅga* that serves as the locus for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) through the exposure of all faults.
This applies to both [cases], provided that one does not overlook the fact that action is independent of non-delayed action.

Or rather, speak in accordance with reality—subduing the opponent’s position and establishing your own—how a seed, even while situated among auxiliary conditions, performs its function as a producer exactly as it did previously, having already determined its status as an agent. But has this not already been stated? Indeed, it has been stated.
For instance—the meaning is that there is no delay regarding the action (*kṛti*).
What is the sense of this: does "no delay" mean that the action occurs immediately after arising, or rather after the gathering of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*)?
Does it mean that as long as there is no gathering of the efficient auxiliary causes, there is no action at all? (8)
Or [it may be called] "the production of the capacity.
In that regard, because there is a lack of evidence for the first and fourth [alternatives],

and because there is uncertainty regarding the second and third, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) alone is the evidence [for the latter two], since [it is observed that] a seed of a particular kind [produces a sprout] upon the occurrence of a subsequent conjunction of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri*).
That "it acts precisely because it possesses the capacity to act" is indeed established by direct perception;
likewise, that "it does not act when deprived of the assembly of auxiliary conditions" is also so established.

And on this point, you yourself have no disagreement, because this is established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and because there is a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary view.
For instance, if something that does not act in the absence of auxiliary causes were likewise not to act even when in conjunction with them, it would be a non-cause of that same kind,
because it fails to act in both cases— both in their presence and in their absence.
Thus, if [it were so] in their conjunction...

Even in their absence, [the effect] would produce it, and thus they would not be causes, because it would be produced even without them. Furthermore, if those things which possess invariable positive and negative concomitance were not causes, it would follow that the effect is causeless;
likewise, its occasional nature would be contradicted.
And thus, if the second position is intended, the very nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity is its non-delayed activity;

if the third position is intended, however, the essential form (*svarūpa*) of an entity is its delayed activity. Therefore, there is no cessation of both modes [of activity]. Alas! This unprecedented display of hypocrisy by him—who, like a *balabhoja* fish dwelling in a lotus pond that is mostly a ground of delusion—torments even his own kinsman, the ornament of truthful speech.

Thus, O friend, do not fear; for by the abundance of your affectionate and charming speech, you have truly supported me—who bears a name identical to your own—without abandoning the company of your companions, who are like a caravan of wealth.
Having cited that very literary work (*sāhitya*), he offers the anecdote of "protecting the cow after it has been sold."

Immediately after such a statement, when the definition [of the means of valid cognition] has been rendered stable, the result of the means of valid cognition is proclaimed as being beneficial by way of its non-instrumentality.

For, since [the object] is characterized by momentary destruction, a discerning person—by virtue of the position of non-delay and so forth—is unable to dismantle even with a mere sketch the ease with which [the object] is experienced at every moment.
Such is the establishment of this capacity.

Therefore, having drawn that very [teaching] from the words of the Teacher into the hollow of the ear with the ladle of hearing, one should rejoice with joy; for even in the field of *sāhitya*, he is not an author in the sense of another's form, since his own nature existed even before.
Thus, it should have been done even previously.
As for what was said by this [author]: [The rest of the passage follows.]
While it is well-established for the proponent that [the opponent] argues according to this method, one might still ask:

"Even so, what is the restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*)? Is it that only an incapable [cause] lacks auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*), or that only a cause capable of acting immediately after acquiring its own nature possesses the concurrence of auxiliaries, and not otherwise?
To this, it is said: Does a certain distinction favorable to the sprout exist in a seed situated in a granary, or does it not, compared to a fragment of stone?

If it were not so, there would be no activity directed toward one thing exclusively, nor would there be cessation for one who desires that [result]. If it is argued that [activity] does indeed exist because it produces, through a succession, a momentary seed capable of generating a sprout—[we ask]: when, then, will it produce such a thing even through a succession?
If it is argued that there is doubt regarding this matter;
Furthermore, what is its nature? Will it produce [the effect] even when those auxiliary conditions are assembled, or not?
Or will it produce it even when they are not assembled, or not?
Now, if it is argued that "it will indeed act precisely when there is the presence of auxiliary conditions," then the doubt arises as to when their presence occurs.
The first [alternative] is not tenable, because there is no room for such a doubt so long as the cause has not been determined in its general capacity.

Or [it is so] because the status of being a cause is determined only when there is room for it; not otherwise, because if there were no room, the true nature of the auxiliary factors could not be determined,
or if there were room, their true nature would not be determined.

In the third case, however, all the seed-moments included within that continuum would necessarily possess the same capacity, because it is a rule that [an effect] arises whenever the collection of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*) is present, and such a collection of auxiliaries is possible everywhere.
If you argue that "the collection of earth and other factors occurs only at a moment that is itself incapable," then is that [moment] not indeed incapable?
In that case, either there is no gathering of auxiliary causes at all,
or even when they are gathered, the production of the effect does not arise from them.
It cannot be the first, because even in a fragment of stone and the like, the conjunction of earth, water, fire, and air is observed.

It cannot be the other [the non-efficient cause], for then there would be the absurd consequence that a sprout might never arise from a seed even when all auxiliary conditions are present, as is the case with a fragment of stone.
If it is argued: "Even so, let it be; what is the fault? (8)
This has not yet been observed.

If you say, "It is merely suspected," then even when that [seed] is present, one might suspect the occurrence of the action despite its absence [of the seed], just as one suspects it when the seed is absent. If you say, "Let it be suspected," then one might likewise suspect it even in the absence of the seed;
and thus, [your position] is excellent. (9)
This is the purification through perception and non-perception.

It might be argued that the objection is not raised by assuming that seeds and other factors produce an effect only when they are in mutual conjunction; for if that were the case, one could determine that all things of that same class possess a single uniform nature due to the necessity of their conjunction.

Nor is it the case that one accepts a capacity existing here and there such that, by means of it, the production of an effect from even incomplete causes would be possible— thereby contradicting perception and non-perception.
Rather, when seeds and other factors are assembled, the production of an effect is conceived by relying on a specific intermediate genus (*avāntarajātiviśeṣa*).

"Since the [effect] can be accounted for by mere observed concomitance (*dṛṣṭasamavadhāna*), there is no evidence for postulating that [additional cause]; thus, there would be the consequence of conceptual over-elaboration (*kalpanāgaurava*).

Furthermore, because [such a cause] is contradicted, because it would entail the abolition of supersensible faculties and so forth, because such a postulation is untenable, and because a particular [cause] must be the motivator of a particular [effect]—that too is insubstantial. For [the capacity for] production in the arising of a seed is..."

The seed alone is the primary cause; although it remains closed within the interior of the husk—concealing the stages beginning with the sprout, the stalk, the bud, and the leaf—it subsequently encounters the conjunction of factors such as the field, the soil, and the application of water, following the sequence of the sickle, the sun, the winnowing basket, the mortar, and the threshing floor.

This process, bound by the causal conditions of its approach, is intended for the time when it is fit to be brought forth, and through a certain succession of transformations, it is finally honored by the full realization of its fruit.

The effect of the earth and other elements, known as the sprout, is not perceived in its entirety [in the seed]; yet this very nature—whether it be the nature of the seed itself, which has undergone a succession of transformations, or that which possesses its former form without falling away—breaks through [the continuity] within that causal series. Thus, preceded by such deliberation, those filled with petty pride declare: "In that regard, for the Buddhists, there is neither an admission of a distinction of universals (*jāti*) that are not different from the object, nor is there a connection with the present context of the treatise."

Furthermore, the established tenet (*siddhānta*) is as follows: that which brings joy to the ears of all the wise arises from its own causes; for instance, if it is asked whence the capable [entity] has arisen, the answer is: from its own causes.
If it is asked, "What do those [impressions] produce in him when no other conditions are present?

Perhaps it might be otherwise, and thus even a single one might sometimes produce [an effect]," [the reply is: although the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*), possessing distinct powers at every moment due to their connection with various successive conditions, continue as a continuum, they may nevertheless appear identical due to some similarity. Nevertheless...

Their nature is indeed distinct; therefore, only a specific thing can be the cause of a specific effect. Why then is this "sṛgalla-pallavita" (the proliferation of trivialities) regarding the perception of differences within perceptible intermediate species? It gratifies the inner mind with such superficiality, like the talk of common folk. For, by means of a gross observation (*sthūla-parāmarśa*), the capacity of a seed—excluded from heterogeneous classes—to produce its own effect is established; yet, even this is [subject to] what is called the investigation of subtle intermediate contingencies and their opposites.

By means of an internal mental operation (*vimarśāntaravṛtti*), that which is established as a specific nature presided over by the state of being a seed (*bījatva*) is proven; what, then, could possibly be untenable in this regard?
Just as, having visualized an object whose essence is situated in a distant place, one determines it to be a "tree" as excluded from non-trees (*avṛkṣavyāvṛtta*). One determines [it].

A person born into the sacrificial tradition of battle, whose specific cognition depends upon proximity, perceives there [in the tree] as "this is a *śiṃśapā*"; yet even while discerning another essential nature—namely, that "the joint of the trunk is composed of a curved hollow and a mass of bark"—he does not conclude that it is devoid of both "treeness" and "*śiṃśapā*-ness.
Nor does he conclude that "every tree is a *śiṃśapā*" or that "all *śiṃśapās* have a trunk-joint composed of a curved hollow and a mass of bark. Such is the case with the subject at hand.

Let there be no derision regarding the removal of the array of objections concerning the reality of things; for the relationship between the probandum and the probans remains unassailed. Indeed, it is not within our scope of acceptance that a universal, such as "seed-ness," exists in a positive form across all individual instances. Furthermore, the claim that one must admit internal, imperceptible distinctions of genus (*jāti*) therein is merely a fabrication of the loquacious; it is not challenged by the mass of evidence. This is like a bee, restless with longing for the fragrance of a lotus situated in the path of the sky.
It penetrates the family of non-existents (*virāva-kula*), namely:
that particularity of birth (*jāti-viśeṣa*) might be inclusive or it might be exclusive; likewise, "rice-ness" (*śālitva*) might be inclusive or it might exclude the rice seedling (*cara*).
Nor is it both, and so forth. (9)

Just as the proliferation of refutations imagined by conceptual construction has not been granted even a seal of approval by the charming smile of your lotus-like smiling face— since no such distinction exists among the various internal classes of things—

so too, although a universal may exist, there is a difference in intrinsic nature (svabhāva-bheda) as it is manifested immediately following the sequence of successive cognitions produced by causes; this has been explained with reasons through the vibration of the knowledge of logic.

Furthermore, as for what is called "repetition" (*punarukti*), it is because there is a contradiction with the causal factor (*prayojaka*) regarding the distinction of a particular; thus, one has begun to prove what is already established.

Nevertheless, even if they were perceived as identical due to some cause, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is nonetheless distinct. This is according to the [authoritative] statement that the final individual instance (*antyavyakti*) characterized by being a rice-seed (*śālibījatva*) and so forth—[is indeed distinct].

The doctrine of an agent is indeed a delusion regarding the specific nature of distinct characteristics; for even the conventional determination of a gross perception directed toward a sprout [presupposes] a seed-substratum that possesses the state of being its agent. When one considers the two states—characterized by the presence or absence of such determinative resolve—the locus and instrument [of action] cannot be conceived even in the slightest degree. Seeing this, those whose pair of feet is honored by the crest-jewels of the circle of authoritative scholars perceive the logical consequence of contradiction and the evidence to the contrary, which acts as an obstacle to [the claim of] identity. Indeed, it is observed [by them].

Thus, even such a momentary discourse is as follows: having considered a Vedic sentence that is either a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or otherwise, one establishes through another means of knowledge (*adhikaraṇa-pramāṇa*) its distinct nature characterized by validity;

or, for example, although the earth, mountains, and so forth are doubtful in their nature—whether they were created by the Moon-god or by someone else—one sets aside that doubt and, by means of another proof, expands upon and understands the truth regarding the many long-standing cycles of conduct to be practiced.
This is the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*). It is firmly established.

Therefore, we consider it logical that whatever, being of such a nature, reproduces its own positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) exactly as they are, possesses causal capacity only for an effect of that same nature;

whereas its specific variations bring about specific differences in the effect, just as in the case of rice and other grains. Since I have stated this by taking up the broad and unerring observation as my primary mark, the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is made to yield its due in that respect—by whom? By one whose intellect is fixed on a coarse vision, having been led astray from the circle of intermediate investigations by thieves.
We state again that it is not by this reasoning [that the seed is non-existent].
Even a seed of a different species, when placed in a granary and not yet sown, is defined as a "seed" because it possesses the nature of a seed.

Since these two states [the sown and the unsown] possess a single, identical intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the claim that the state of being a non-seed follows merely from the logical reason (*prayojaka*)—as asserted through invalid means of knowledge such as the *prasaṅga*—is stated in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) with what intention?
However, the stability of that which exists in those two states is established by perception.
Now, this might be so, with the intention that there is some specific distinction belonging to it;
or else, having considered that neither the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) nor its converse amounts to anything at all.

Alternatively, one might consider whether "seed-ness" itself is the universal (*sāmānya*), whose form is fully present in each individual instance of its own class, which is designated as both an innate capacity and an adventitious capacity, and which, when conjoined with auxiliary factors, is perceived as capable of producing a sprout; yet, having reflected on the fact that stability is not established by perception— since it is void of such a nature— the first [position] is not tenable.

But you are also like that, [arising] only from seeds that are at the very limit; thus, the second [position] is also not tenable. Furthermore, the proof consisting of the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*viparyaya*), which has all objections completely refuted, [remains valid].

Through the transformation (*parāvṛtti*) of the non-seed, the state of being a seed will be determined even in that which is generally accepted as unmanifest, with respect to the seed at both prior and subsequent times. Therefore, the mere demonstration of distinction between this position and the position of intrinsic (*nija*) and adventitious (*āgantuka*) powers is no protection. As for the consequence that the sprout would lack a restriction of genus and causal efficiency—that is not a subverting argument against the opposite view; for [the state of being a seed] exists through a specific transformation of the non-seed.
This is because the rule regarding the sprout's skin is logically established.
By this, it is also stated that the contrary [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For it is specifically a particular seed that is the efficient cause, not the mere seed alone, due to the force of the operation of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the seed.

Having established it thus from a coarse perspective, there is no loss of conventional practice; however, the means for proving the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is fraught with difficulties. For the restriction of the birth of a sprout cannot be without a cause, as that would lead to the absurd consequence of its occurring everywhere.
Nor can it have another [external] cause, because such a thing does not exist. This [is the case]. (2)

When [the reason], being possessed of its characteristic mark, turns away from the opposite class, it rests precisely upon the seed’s status as a causal factor by grasping its own pervader; thus is the establishment of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) described. This is because the specific nature (*svabhāvabheda*) residing in the state of being a seed, by way of being characterized by another state, functions as the restrictive cause for the necessity of sprout-hood.
Even in the case of a variable [cause], the mere state of being a seed is not the causal factor for a sprout; rather, it is the very nature of being a seed that is the causal factor.

Furthermore, when one observes a seed functioning while governed by its own nature and governed by all remaining conditions, this is what is understood as "being a seed"—this is a coarse conceptualization.
That is not a fully established fruit, for the locus of reality has not been scrutinized; thus, [the claim] "this very thing is you" is not a discourse concerning the ultimate truth.

When the investigation has been introduced in this way, how could the discussion fail to expand upon the occasion? Consequently, is the nature of the seed the cause of efficacy toward some effect, or not?
If the seed does not have that nature, [then it cannot be the cause].

Because nothing at all is of use in that form, and thus the nature of being a seed, which is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), does not exist, while the particularity (*viśeṣa*)—which is beyond the scope of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—does exist; such is the "pure intellect" (*viśuddhā buddhiḥ*). This is a state of mockery, for it mocks the very state [of reality].
It does not exclude [the others] from being causes;
rather, when there is utility in some respect, all are indistinguishable in that form because they possess that same nature.
Even if they are perceived as having similar forms due to some similarity, nevertheless, these [individuals] are indeed distinct. (8)

By the statement that "the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of something is the cause of something else," and by what was said regarding the fact that a thing would exist as such [in its own nature], that too remains as a well-known fallacy; for it is not the case that the capacity characterized by the transformation into specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) arises from the presence of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), because it lacks the final seed-form (*antyabījarūpa*).
Indeed, that very [nature] is neither prior nor posterior; therefore, what is the point of this? Consequently, there is a different [nature] at every moment.
Having relied upon the completeness of conditions conducive to the effect, the intermediate state of being a seed—which has its own nature as its objective support—is perceived;

it is perceived as being such with respect to that single effect. That very thing, being such with respect to that single effect, is the efficient cause (*prayojaka*); this is the grasping of the non-existent [cause], as has been stated by him, and thus: (2)
A seed performs only its own specific effect and not others.
Nor is that effect merely the thing-in-itself, for that would entail the consequence of it being produced even from what is not a seed.
Nor is it merely the seed, for that would entail the consequence of it being produced even by that which causes a sprout [but is not the seed].
Nor can it be any single factor among those [causes] such as the sprout, because that would entail the consequence of the effect arising even before they have arisen.

If you argue that whenever a thing has arisen and rests within the midst of auxiliary conditions conducive to a particular effect, then that very thing is the efficient cause (*prayojaka*) for that effect; then, does this apply by virtue of an intermediate specific genus (*jāti-bheda*), or rather by the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the seed?

Or [if you say] it is the first case: then that very difference in genus (*jātibheda*) is the determinant there; what, then, has come of the nature of being a seed (*bījatva*)? But in the second case, it follows that even for things of identical character, there is non-production due to the variation of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*);
for when combined with their respective auxiliaries, the seed-nature—which is the determinant for each respective effect—is common to all of them.

Here too, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is not employed for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in a certain form does not possess that form; for example, a seed is not of the nature of a sprout when it is not performing any function as a sprout. Likewise, rice seeds and the like, having entered into the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), are not employed for causal efficiencies by way of being seeds [in isolation]. This is a *prasaṅga*-reason based on the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), because possessing that form is pervaded by being capable of causal efficiency.
Otherwise, there would be an over-extension [of the principle].
If it is argued that its very nature as such cannot be denied because it is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then let the reverse be the case:
whatever has a certain nature is capable of performing causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) by means of that nature.

Just as entities contained within a causal complex possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), so too these things such as seeds situated in a granary and so forth belong to the class of seeds; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), because the capacity [to produce] is invariably concomitant with that very form. Consequently, there exists some effect in which the seed is produced. Such profound arguments at the outset—like the bolt of Kaṇera, or the opening of a conch-shell horn—are [the means of proof].
—O fool, tell me, from where have you derived this continuous sequence, or this constructed argument, based on such fallacious reasoning?

For the consequence beginning with "by means of the successive conjunction of various conditions" according to the doctrine of Dharmakīrti—which is renowned for its synthesis of the views of preeminent masters of irreproachable knowledge—is not logically consistent with the [opponent's] position.
This is because mere similarity in form lacks the necessary pervasion (*vyāpti*), as it is incapable of producing effects such as sprouts and the like in the manner of a real entity.
Because of the absence of a cause, a capable intrinsic nature is untenable.

For instance, in that case, the collection consisting of the location, the seed, the earth, and so forth—provided there is no obstruction—is the cause capable of producing a homogeneous sprout; whereas that which is the specific condition for their mutual proximity and support is [the cause of the sprout's diversity].

That [cause] is capable of producing that effect; and since those [capacities] do not exist prior to, after, or separately [from it], the defects that arise from priority, posteriority, or separateness do not apply even to those things that are capable. Therefore, for that which is the efficient cause—namely, the cause of their mutual approach and so forth—there is never any alteration.

By this principle, the specific determination of the relation between cause and effect is to be seen everywhere among those [things] which, moment by moment, are characterized by a succession of distinct and varying intrinsic natures.

However, this applies to things whose capacities are subject to change, and not to things that possess a stable, single nature, because it is impossible for such an intrinsic nature to undergo alteration.
This is because an entity with a capacity-nature and one with a non-capacity-nature cannot both be engaged in action and non-action simultaneously.
If it is argued that "it acts when accompanied by something else," then why does it not act alone? If you say it does not act alone, is its nature incapable of producing the effect?
"What can one who is capable not do?

(7) "If he does not act, how can he be called capable?"—thus [the author], whose intellect was practiced, has presented the words of the teacher Hetubindu, which, though as stainless as the spotless moon, appear as if thrown into disorder by a multitude of obstacles, as if they had mounted a vehicle for the sake of carrying out his own position. (8) pā-... [text fragment]

Having superposed the condition of literary composition (*sāhitya*) as a conceptual construct, you attempt to quell the expectation of a consequence or its opposite by considering capacity and incapacity; yet even there, the Master’s statement remains:
"Even in the case of literary composition, the agent exists in the form of another, and its own nature existed even prior [to that]. Therefore, it would have to act even before.
Thus, even in the case of "sāhitya" (co-occurrence), it follows as a consequence that the capacity for causal efficiency (*karaṇasāmarthya*) is not a qualifier of *sāhitya*.
Therefore, unless the previously stated sentence is established as being grounded in its own nature, one cannot accept the logical connection of the members [of the syllogism] as having been stated.

Now, if momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) were indeed the case, then even this most venerable author of the treatise, upon encountering the application of the very means of valid cognition that establish it, would be reduced to the playful state of a lecherous woman; for his slippery, trivial, and impure meaning—swollen with the mass of fallacious arguments—becomes loathsome even to those who are most excellent and wise. (2)

This is not surprising; for even if the Lord of the Gods were to watch with a thousandfold concentration while being squeezed, he would not perceive the seed’s capacity to produce [the sprout] in any state other than its own—such as its persistence or non-persistence—due to the arrangement of those states. Thus, on the view that things are permanent, how can this restriction be brought to honor? Is it not rather due to the fact that even the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) has its limits set by its own causes?

Or whether it appears as incapable due to the lack of individual efficacy, or as a state of confusion regarding the limits of what has been reached due to the deficiency of its own nature, or as being devoid of the manifestation of past and present karma— whether seen or unseen— due to the absence of its causal basis; if that is so, how could anyone proceed forward from the expansion of such meaningless initial discourse,
as if walking toward a precipice?

Or [the view] that it goes only to heaven—these are five positions based on the postulation of the five sense-faculties. Or, because of the determination of objects other than those accumulated and prepared, the discerning one enters into the mind as food and so forth; thus it is possible to establish even what is untrue, such as form being produced by its own collection of causes, which is perceived by the eye as "this is my form. Then, as sound approaches, he weighs it by means of his own self; and in another case, regarding other objects in this manner—(7)
—[If it were] to be thus instructed, then the fivefold conceptualization regarding the objects of apprehended things would be ultimately real; for [the senses] are capable of producing a substance.

Indeed, because its boundaries are established by its own causes, that which is a single [entity], possessing specific qualities ordained by its own causes, either sustains a single cognition or five cognitions through the clarity of the fivefold manifold sense-faculties, such as the eye and so forth. Immediately thereafter, even that which is practiced as non-injurious (is what should be cultivated).

Since each [cause] individually possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), those who proclaim the mere destruction or transformation of other things have begun an unpleasant counter-argument against what is pleasant;

for they do not accept the skillful craftsmanship of karma as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). One must therefore establish that the entire collection of entities, such as seeds and so forth, is produced within the interior of space.
If that [cognition] is admitted to be attached to what is seen, then let it wait for another [instance] as you wish;
however, the restriction [of its being non-conceptual] is contradicted—thus there stands a preeminent blow from a proof that severely hinders [your position].
Furthermore, if one speaks of a new type of debate such as *vāda* and so forth, there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of defeat due to distraction (*vikṣepa-nigraha*). (2)
It may be that in the final similar instance (*sapakṣa*), only the manifestation of the worship of the position (*pakṣa*) is observed, and nothing further.
Therefore, just as that entity is the cause of that [effect] in such a way, it is likewise the non-cause of that; by what means is it not accepted as a non-cause, while being considered a cause? (3)
Without a difference in intrinsic nature, even causal activity is not tenable;
because that which is eternal lacks any distinction [from its prior state], its capacity [to act] is difficult to establish.

Thus, the expansion of the argument through the application of the *prasaṅga* and its reversal (*tadviparyaya*) establishes that the final transformation of a specific grain, which has been determined to be a producer while remaining stable, is unshakeable; this is the established position of the Teacher’s word, because it is impossible for that nature to become otherwise.
However, for that which possesses such a property, its becoming so [as it does] is as unavoidable as its state in the final moment.
If the capacity arises for that which was previously incapable, then if that capacity is its very nature (*tatsvabhāvatva*), it is simply the production of something new (*apūrvotpatti*).
If it is not its nature, then it remains non-productive even afterwards, just as it was before.
[This is the sixth point concerning] the distinct category of things called "capacity" (*sāmarthya*).

Because it arises from its own cause, an entity possesses an established nature; it is produced by causes, but not as something lacking a fixed foundation. However, when the completeness of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri*) is present, the seed—though dependent on uncertain and dense causal bonds—is produced by its own cause with a well-considered probability. Thus, according to the logic of all principles, this [entity] is indeed produced.
For dependence is indeed a relation; when [a thing] is already established, what dependence could there be?
Therefore, in reality, no relation exists for any entity whatsoever.
For relation is a conjunction within form; how could it occur when duality is absent?
Therefore, in reality, there is no connection between the elements and the various [derived] things.
Even if dependence were a relation, how could that which is non-existent depend?
And how could an existent thing, being already established and free from desire, depend?

Because there is an absence of mutual dependence between the established (*siddha*) and the unestablished (*asiddha*), their relationship is absolutely impossible. For that which is already established possesses nothing whatsoever for the sake of which it would depend on the unestablished—just as an entity such as a sprout depends on the unestablished in its particular aspect while being established in its universal aspect.

This is because they are distinct due to the superimposition of contradictory properties, namely completion and non-completion, and thus do not transcend the dichotomy of the established and the unestablished.

Therefore, there is no possibility for a collection of entities such as dependence on auxiliary causes, strength, or the waxing and waning phases; for this [entity], being constrained by the very shackles of its own production from its cause, does not even utter a word, remaining bound by a vow of silence like a man who has taken a formal oath of silence.

Therefore, it is precisely an object that is contrary to valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which is made known by a signifier (*jñāpaka*), and it is precisely what is to be produced by a causal factor (*kāraka-hetu*); this alone is the supreme practice of those who rely on valid cognition. As for what was stated: "Alternatively, there is a formulation by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): 'The seed under dispute lacks the effect, such as a sprout, when its auxiliary conditions are absent, because it belongs to the same class of seeds that are the objects of the certainty regarding the production of that [effect]. "
Furthermore, that which is not produced as an effect such as a sprout when deprived of auxiliary causes does not belong to such a class [of causal things],
just like a fragment of stone; this point is already established by the argument that even when accompanied [by auxiliaries], it does not act in the form of another.
It has already been established that in the prior state, the seed is one from which the nature of producing a sprout has not yet departed, and thus the new shoot has not yet manifested.

Having integrated this into the basis of coarse conceptualization, the construction of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding the seed— which is distinguished from what is non-seed— is [applied] to the subtle state.
Even one whose mind is struck down by the investigation of other [arguments] must consider: who here is debating?

Therefore, with respect to a coarse examination, if its deficiency in producing the effect of a sprout were not established through the loss of its specific nature, then it would not be an inconclusive [reason].
The state of being of a certain kind, which is unestablished from the perspective of subtle investigation,
is precisely that which does not exist as its producer;
the meaning is that it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
In this regard, existence is the ultimate reality;

but how can there be a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) for the reason [of momentariness], namely the cloud? That [cloud] must be established as possessing the property to be proven by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and that valid cognition consists in the reversal of a reductio (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*). Furthermore, what function is being attributed to that [reversal]?

Having taken as its object the performance and non-performance of an action observed by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the prior and posterior states— and whether by way of sublation by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or by the logical principle that "that which is occasional does not depend [on anything else]" according to the words of the Teacher [Dignāga] on the secret of reasoning (*tarkopaniṣad*)— the [reasoning] establishes the performance and non-performance [of the seed], which is contradictory to its unity, since the individual agency was observed in the seed at the end of each state.

Since the wise one, while explaining the general definition of contradiction (*virodha*), is concerned with its specific aspects, the general definition therein is the necessity of non-coexistence within a single substratum (*ekadharmi*). And that generality would be specified by two modes:
that characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) and that termed the state of existing through mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthiti*).

In that regard, for the first [position], existence is established by means of perceptions and non-perceptions; for the second, however, it is established either through the proof of mutual exclusion, like the destruction of a constant entity, or through sublation by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By the statement "like that which is occasional and independent," two methods have been set forth.

In that case, the capacity to act at that specific time is established as being contradictory to the capacity to act at a different time; it is not [contradictory] by virtue of acting at another time, because this affirmation is not sublated by such a restriction.
Just as occurrence at a particular time is contradictory to non-occurrence at a particular time, so too is independence contradictory to dependence.

Furthermore, by that very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the fact that [the two properties]—being occasional and being independent—are not established simultaneously within a single substratum (*ekadharmī*) is determined;

by that very same means, their contradiction is ascended upon the palace of understanding. Likewise, through the distinction of time, there is the means for understanding the non-contradiction between the property of being non-dependent and so forth.

Furthermore, he [the opponent] sets forth the unimpaired definition of a means of valid cognition known as *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) and its contrapositive (*viparyaya*), which demonstrates the rule that two mutually contradictory properties cannot coexist in a single substratum. Thus, the opponent has fled out of hope; therefore, whatever else the proponent said in this manner also retreats like a shattered shell, along with his ministers.
Let the very state of being a seed be the determining factor; let it be that a thing possesses the nature of an agent when its auxiliary conditions are present,
and thus let its non-acting also be logically consistent when those conditions are absent.

If it is argued: "Even so, this determination applies only to that which belongs to the same class (*tajjātīya*), and not to a single individual where there is the imposition of contradictory properties characterized by performing and not performing [an action];
and thus, in the absence of that [class-character], it is unavoidable because it is established by perception"—[we reply]: No, for you have failed to understand the nature of contradiction.
For that [contradiction] must consist either in the two properties being of the nature of mutual negation (*parasparābhāva*), like the eternal and the non-eternal; or...

Alternatively, [the reason] might consist in being the producer of that [contradiction] in the subject (*dharmin*), like coldness and heat, or in possessing that [contradiction], like having a staff or having a crest-ring.
It cannot be the first, because [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) when devoid of qualifications, since something is produced as long as it exists;
however, in the case of [the reason] with qualifications, there is the establishment of contradiction—(4)
—because superimposition is untenable.

For when there is the non-performance of a certain action at a particular time, that is the absence of its performance at that time, but not the absence of its performance at another time; nor do we maintain the coexistence of these two within a single substratum.
Not the other [alternative], because of the contradiction between existence and non-existence.

Because the performance or non-performance [of an action] by two things that are not distinct is unestablished; for performance and non-performance are indeed the presence or absence of auxiliary causes—otherwise designated as "activity"—or the presence or absence of the effect.
Even if distinctness were established, performance at its own time would imply the absence of non-performance, just as it excludes its own non-existence, but not at another time.
For that which does not exist at a certain time cannot, at that time, exclude its own nature.
—thus, in order to cast doubt upon the absence of contradiction, [it would follow that] if that were so, it would never exist there, nor would anything ever be its opposite.
It would follow that "the existence of the non-existent is not found, nor is the non-existence of the existent found," or else there would be no contradiction at all.

Such irrationality on the part of a logician does not appease the mind, which moves with the harshness born from contact with the sun's rays, because these false conceptualizations are devoid of any basis in reality.

Furthermore, even if one were to address the reversal of the logical consequence (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*) by means of a single statement— let it be so— even then, contradiction cannot exist between those two [capacities] when the distinction of time is not intended, regardless of whether they are capable or incapable.
It is established [as such] because it is impossible to draw a conclusion [in that manner].

If it is argued that, disregarding "when" or "then," one can conclude that "whatever is capable necessarily performs [the action]," we say no; for if the restriction of time is not intended, it would follow that "whatever is capable performs [the action] at some time or other."

And likewise, in the case of a rule of possibility (*sambhava-vidhi*), absolute non-connection (*atyantāyoga*) is what is contradicted, not mere non-connection (*ayoga*). This is like saying "the lotus is indeed blue"; it is blue, but not necessarily so at all times. That too [is accepted], because even by excluding absolute non-connection, it is intended that agency (*kartṛtva*) might occur as long as the seed exists, as in the case of a "soiled lotus" (*malinanalina*).
— it must be examined as a semblance.
And as it has been said: "Is it not the case that what was previously incapable..."

Whence has its capacity come even later? If it were not capable at first, it could not have acquired it later; this is not so, because [capacity] arises from possessing those respective auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
For capacity is indeed the state of being a producer of that [effect].
Whether [the cause] possesses those [auxiliaries] or possesses others, its lack of agency—that is, its incapacity—is its innate nature.

This too has been resolved by examining the seed of production as being dependent on auxiliaries; and since those auxiliaries occur at different times due to the conditions for their own approach, it follows that the effects also occur at different times. Nevertheless, the entity itself is produced and perishes at one and the same time; therefore, at that moment, the effect—
Let it act as soon as it has arisen, because that is its very nature.

If it is argued that this is like [the action of] one situated in a single location— whether this simultaneity is with respect to the time of its own nature or with respect to the presence of auxiliary causes— in the first case, nothing is untenable.

Since even eternal things possess this very nature, and because entities consist solely of the present moment, the distinction is simply that in some cases it is limited by a temporal boundary (*sāvadhi*) and in others it is unlimited (*niravadhi*).
Even when there is a limit, [the distinction lies in] the excellence or lack thereof in the flow of activity and its fruit.
This is the distinction from the two sages.
However, the second [type] might also occur if there were simultaneity among them;
but it has been stated that the auxiliary causes are successive.

If one says that [the cause] produces [the effect] by its very nature while accompanied by auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), then for a speaker who has lost their senses, the consequence would follow that it must produce [the effect] even when those factors have perished; such is the unrestrained babble of a child. Enough of this.
Therefore, since the time of the effect is one and the time of the cause is another, the conventional designation "prior time" is used in relation to the time of the related factor.

This too is a vast and false fabrication, a vessel for the pain of a multitude of thorns, resulting from the rejection of the qualification of the completeness of auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-sākalya*).

However, agency and non-agency perceived through spatial distinction do not incur contradiction and the like, as they depend upon the exclusion of other [conditions] and are accompanied by their own inherent nature.

By that very same auxiliary cause, at that very same time, and in that very same manner, let there be both relatedness and unrelatedness; for it is not determined whether this occurs at a prior or a subsequent moment.

Let it be, then, that there is both a relation and a non-relation of that very thing with that very same auxiliary cause—this is a contradiction, [we reply] no, because the conceptual alternatives are untenable.
For instance, in one related entity [the presence of] another related entity would contradict either its own nature of absence,
or its being the counter-positive of that absence,
or its being accompanied by the phrase "at that very time."
In that very case, is it accompanied [by the other], or accompanied by both, or likewise accompanied in that same way?
The process of conceptualization (vikalpa),
the explanation of its extraction, and the examination thereof must be stated;
for instance, in the case of a rabbit's horn.
And those who are either fit or unfit are likewise born.
"Since there is a contradiction with its conceptual differentiation for that which has an eternally fit nature,
let this very nature of fitness be described;
what is the use of other [qualities] such as motion and so forth?"
Even though those [entities] exist, [the expression] "belonging to that" [is not possible],
because the relationship is unestablished.

If, according to the principle that "this difference in intrinsic nature (svabhāva-bheda) is appropriate for those things born at every moment," the seed's own intrinsic nature— which is capable of conjunction— never departs [from it], then how can it be said that its state of possessing its own intrinsic nature is not caused by anything other than itself, such as grass, and that there is no other causal activity?
But as for the remainder—excluding that which is insignificant—it belongs to one whose childhood is unrestrained, and so forth;
[this refers] to that light.
Now, if that nature is merely occasional, let its very basis be investigated... [as it is said in the commentary: "What is the use of anything further? [this is stated] out of a sense of sarcasm.

"Thus ends the second chapter, the determination of the existence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) and so forth, which refutes that which was already rejected by the inference of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) through the method of positive concomitance (*anvaya*)."
The secret of the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*viparyaya*)... [previously] established...
has been described as being excluded from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), namely the non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*).
Furthermore, in that regard, there is an excess concerning the locus (*āśraya*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
There is an absence of valid cognition regarding [an unreal object],
because the operation of a valid cognition does not apply to a non-entity, and because if a valid cognition were to operate upon it, its unreality would be untenable.

If it is argued that, in that case, there is a contradiction with one's own words regarding non-conventional usage (*avyavahāra*), then does this contradiction with one's own words serve as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for those [non-conventional usages]?
For in that case, even the conventional usage consisting in the negation of conventional usage would be undermined;
or else, one would necessarily have to accept a conventional usage that lacks any basis in valid cognition.

Not the first; for even with a thousand contradictions, it is impossible to demonstrate either perception or inference regarding that which is permanent, or regarding the absence of succession and so forth, or regarding a rabbit’s horn. If such were possible, then enough with this quarreling of fools. But as for the second [alternative], it is indeed accepted by those who rely on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇika*).
In that case, silence is obtained; what can we do?
Where speech is entirely inappropriate, silence is better; you too should reflect upon this for a moment.

Between one who is silent regarding a matter that lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and one who speaks at length, which is better? It is the one who possesses valid cognition. If you say: "Even though you are wise, you did not remain silent, but rather prohibited linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) by asserting that it does not exist when it is unreal"—this is true. However, [you did so] thinking, "Let there be no occasion for an unreal object that contradicts its own words," and thus, while you yourself [asserted] that which is unreal...

— Just as conventional usage is accepted [by you] despite its lack of ultimate validity, so too do we, considering that in our investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) conventional usage lacking such validity must not be rendered impossible, accept this contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) precisely as lacking ultimate validity.
However, if you were to maintain an equal view toward both cases, then we too would have nothing further to say.

But as for the third [position], it is both without a basis in valid cognition (*apramāṇika*) and yet something that must necessarily be accepted; so you yourself must be asked, "Whose command is this?
If you say, "Because conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) is very firmly established," then there is a contradiction: to be without a basis in valid cognition and yet to be firmly established.

If it is argued that [the opponent's position] is established in some way or another—[we reply: if it lacks epistemic warrant (*aprāmāṇika*), it cannot be established in any way whatsoever; therefore, let that very point [of its lack of warrant] be stated, for such is the established rule (*vyavasthā*) in debate (*vāda*).

However, in the case of mere wrangling (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), the inquiry into the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone determines the outcome; thus, there is a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavyāghāta*).

In that case, (10) it is impossible to provide a reply by means of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*); however, if one attempts to reply by means of what is not a valid means of cognition, there is a defeat (*bhaṅga*) by one's own very words, because one has already admitted for oneself that there is no valid means of cognition regarding the questions and so forth stated by me. Furthermore, in the case of failing to reply, it is simply a lack of presence of mind (*apratibhā*).

If the avoidance of contradiction were possible by accepting conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), then it might indeed be accepted; however, this is not the case. For it has been stated by the opponent that "being the locus of all conventional usage and being the locus of its negation are not mutually contradictory"—but all of this is inconsistent. Indeed, by pointing out the non-establishment [of the reason] based on the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) in order to demonstrate the self-contradiction of one's own words, the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "failing to point out a fault" (*adoṣodbhāvana*) is raised.
(3) If it is asked how so, it is said:
the thesis to be established is that there is an absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the example of the substratum (*āśraya*) and so forth;
the reason (*hetu*) adduced is "because valid cognition does not operate with respect to a non-entity (*avastu*)."

Thus, by way of this "patter" (i.e., the argument), the logical justification has been set forth: when the locus (*āśraya*) has been established as a support through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and when the property (*dharma*) characterized by the non-operation of a means of valid cognition is established as being a property of the subject (*dharmidharmatva*),
how could there not be an understanding of the non-establishment of the locus and so forth?
