Now, if it is argued that there is indeed no fault such as "unestablished" (*asiddhi*) and so forth— since even the opponent's means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is unestablished, and thus cannot be brought to bear in the proof and so on— it follows that that very [opponent's] cognition is [itself] devoid of any contradiction (*apavāda*).

Furthermore, regarding that which you called a "refutation" where there was no fault, this is what is termed the "pointing out of a non-fault" as a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Therefore, since the debate has already reached its conclusion by the refutation of one of the two disputants, why should there be any further pointless threefold conceptualization? For instance, what proof would have been demonstrated? No proof at all has been demonstrated, because the faultlessness of one's own means of proof [is established] through the manifestation of the opponent's statement.
Because [the opponent] is deluded, there is a deviation from his own words.

Furthermore, the refutation of the conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) that negates non-conventional practice is itself sublated by his own speech, due to the presence of the negation of conventional practice. Moreover, for the opponent, the property of the subject (*dharmin*) is established as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, the cause for the conventional practice of negating conventional practice is not discarded, but rather placed directly into his hand; indeed, it is the very conventional practice of negating conventional practice.

Thus, even for a wanderer (janaṅgama), the conventional practice of asserting the absence of the pervaded (vyāpyābhāva) through the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalambha)— which is so heart-warming— is something that must necessarily be accepted as a conventional practice, even if it is very far removed from the practice of those who possess valid cognition (prāmāṇika).
Furthermore, as for what was said, "not even by a thousand contradictions," and so forth, that too should be understood as being constrained by its own internal contradiction.

Regarding an eternal entity, it is impossible to demonstrate a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whether it be perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*). Do you accept this, or do you not?
And as for your acceptance, is it by means of a valid cognition or an invalid one?

If [the opponent] understands by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is a contradiction with his own words; but if he understands by means of what is not a valid cognition, then this is the understanding of one who lacks valid cognition—
this is a great distortion.
Nor is this a mere quarrel of fools, because the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) of valid cognition has already been demonstrated.

As for the second [position], it appears as something accepted; thus, by saying "the person is authoritative" (*prāmāṇika*), they are themselves refuting the linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) regarding the negation of conventions concerning non-entities. By means of that very linguistic convention which negates the convention regarding a specific object—namely, the non-operation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) toward that object—they have stated that the aforementioned probandum (*sādhya*) has that [non-entity] as its object.
It is difficult to establish [a proof].

Regarding a non-entity (*avastu*), whether one attempts to establish the negation of conventional discourse (*vyavahāra-pratiṣedha*), the refutation of conventional discourse (*vyavahāra-khaṇḍana*), the expression of that which is inexpressible by words (*aśabda-vācya*), or the establishment of the negation of the negation of conventional discourse, they all result in being contradicted by one's own words (*svavāg-bādhā*). Since these fallacies bring about the destruction of the present argument, the purpose [of the opponent] is already accomplished. Thus ends [the section on] the fault.

Because the proponent of non-apprehension is necessarily refuted by the opponent, that which was stated—namely, "What is the point of speech in this case? It is entirely useless," and so forth—is also pursued, followed, and carried out as being self-contradictory.
Or, if one fails to respond out of fear of this [refutation], it constitutes some form of *aprati-bhā* (inability to reply).

—nor is there any ground for the eclipse of the power of the sun-like [proponent’s] influence even when [the argument] is in its middle stage; thus, he is one who has utterly transcended internal calamities and speaks with authority.

For instance, when the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is again raised by the opponent as a refutation, it becomes difficult to maintain because it partakes in the state of non-utterance.

Since this is a ground for defeat due to the absence of *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity), it merely illuminates the proof established by the virtuous, which is like the light of the sun; thus, the conclusion of the debate is indeed attained.
Whether by being contradicted by his own words, by being defeated, or by the exhaustion of his eloquence, a proponent who either fails to speak or speaks incorrectly is censured.

Furthermore, when he adopts a discourse through the artful devices of his own language that are disconnected, yet does not admit the fault in what has been said, and instead proclaims, "The assembly of listeners [perceives] a mere quivering of words," and claims,
"It is true that according to valid cognition, the object is self-contradictory," and so forth— that too is a hollow deception worthy of ridicule.

The practice of negating a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra-pratiṣedha-vyavahāra*) is not excessively overextended precisely because it is not contradicted by one's own words; however, we do not accept this practice [of negation] on the grounds that "let such a thing not exist. Rather, there is the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya-viraha*) due to the absence of its pervader (*vyāpaka-viraha*), which is distinguished as being in accordance with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-anugata*). This is because the relationship of pervader and pervaded is established by its own means of valid cognition, and thus for that which is devoid of it [the pervader], [there follows the absence of the pervaded].
Furthermore, since they have accepted a subject (*dharmin*) that lacks real existence,

and because that which is non-existent cannot possibly undergo the transfer of the various grammatical cases (*kāraka-kalā*) intended for such entities as substrata (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth— otherwise, how could these Naiyāyikas, who pride themselves on their knowledge of logic, avoid being blocked by the contradiction of their own words through such gross errors?
For, in the face of a contradiction with their own words, they have presented their own statement as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) that serves as a refutation.
Therefore, why do you call this [objection] "unauthoritative"? Relinquish your desire to tie up the knots of the "Void" (śūnya) treatise.

For in that case, even if you accept that your own words contradict themselves—which is unauthoritative—you do not thereby abandon the fact that it is a contradiction of your own words; for instance, when you say, "Inference is not a valid means of knowledge. If you claim there is no fault simply because you have accepted it, then let it be the same in other cases as well. We too shall say: "We accept that there is 'unestablishedness' (asiddhatva) regarding objects that are non-entities," even though [these arguments] arise through mere verbal wrangling and cavil (jalpa-vitaṇḍā).
Since it is also stated [in that way], the intended fault is cast aside with respect to that position;
[this refers to the phrase] "of one who is engaged merely in questioning the means of valid cognition regarding the thesis and so forth," and so on.

By that talkative person, who seeks victory and asks about the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), something has been undertaken that deals with non-existent entities; and that which was asked does not establish itself.
But if its establishment is achieved through conceptual construction,
then once the question has been posed,
the fundamental reason— having found its opportunity— will manifest effectively.

By asserting, "From what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which has a non-existent thing as its subject (*avastudharmin*) established?", one is in fact questioning the means of valid cognition that would have a non-existent thing as its subject. Since that [subject] is not established through a means of valid cognition, such a question lacks any basis and is as trivial as the perception of a mere blade of grass on the surface of a threshing floor; how then is this not contradicted by one's own words?

For, from the question regarding a means of valid cognition whose object is a particularity (*viśeṣa*), that particularity is established; for if it were not established, an inquiry into its object would be impossible.

If one accepts [the opponent's] proof, then by that very speech which is supremely sweet in its ultimate sense, one destroys one's own position; thus, being destroyed, how can there be a contradiction with one's own words even in the case of *kathā* (debate) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil)?
Therefore, when the Buddhist has thus presented the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) for the sake of the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpyābhāva*), for whom—
Even for me, victory arises when [the opponent] is shattered by one's own words;

if he does not speak, he falls into the vast terrain of *apratibhā* (inability to respond). Thus, enough with this bodily vow! By the very logic of the situation, let it be accepted that even a non-entity (*avastu*)—as a subject (*dharmin*)—has as its object its own complete set of properties (*nijadharma*), which are established through a corresponding determination (*nirūpaṇa*) based on properties appropriate to itself.

O members of the assembly, it is thus: while the body lives, the designation "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña) is applied as a means for making known that which is to be illustrated; its status as a means of valid cognition and so forth has been established.

Its prowess is proclaimed through pure negative concomitance (kevalavyatireka), so that it may not be equal to [the fallacy of] audibility (śrāvaṇatva). Therefore, it must be described as being excluded from the similar instance (sapakṣa); otherwise, the false assertion that it would result in its existence within the similar instance would shine forth [as a fallacy].
One might think: "Its status as a purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) reason is lost because of a lack of mental satisfaction, since there is no similar instance (sapakṣa).
Therefore, its presence in that [similar instance]—which was previously introduced as being undesirable—must be rejected. If one objects thus, [we reply:

Does he indicate the absence of the reason's presence in the similar instance by means of denying its existence in something non-existent? If not, then even the linguistic usage of negating both existence and non-existence would be a mere linguistic negation.
Thus, what is it that is negated by the term "non-exclusion" (*nivṛtti*)?
It is the possession of breath and so forth, because these exist in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
It is not excluded, because the state of being the source (*apādānatva*) is absent [in the dissimilar instances].
This very dialectical practice of the Naiyāyika shines forth, rooted in the refutation and removal of objections against the *vyatireka* (negative-only) reason.

Declare that it is not merely bound by compliance with the opposition initiated by the Buddhists; rather, state some beautiful and charming principle consisting of merit for this weapon of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

By which [reason], when its presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) has disturbed the expansion of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), it is perceived as having the property of being established (*siddhadharmitayā*); and this [subject] depending upon that would then have the property of being absent (*avidyamānatva*) superimposed as the "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*).

Furthermore, there would be for this [absent thing] a pursuit of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth, even if only by the slightest degree; for that which is non-existent cannot be the recipient of words such as "gold," which are based on causes designated as "potency" (*śakti*).
With white eyes, like a mass of white lotuses in the sky;

with the deep rumble of unseasonable clouds; now, [he is] not one who can be overcome by those skilled in policy, for he has begun the means for awakening to the objects of knowledge, which is free from calamity and possesses the vision of the objects of knowledge that are devoid of faults.

— With her anger somewhat diminished, she approaches. Without entering this house of wonder, how can you, who have not yet established the means for rectifying pride, conceal the sequence of the present distinction by masking it with a mere semblance of discourse— a discourse that is a futile torment, which serves as the proof for establishing the non-existence of the object of cognition, and whose capacity has been cultivated through the extensive conventional usage of non-existence?

This path, which leads from the gone and the not-yet-gone, is manifold for those who possess the cause [of wisdom]. By means of the removal of the delusion regarding the "good," one should here examine the body; it is capable of washing away the stains of envy, anger, and partisan talk.

What is the use of examining the beauty or ugliness of a eunuch for a woman who desires him?
For whether that object of a word be an existent or a non-existent thing, if it either obstructs or accomplishes some human goal according to one's inclination by virtue of its true nature,

then— while striving based on the conceptual construction that it is the cause for achieving the desired end at that very moment— one who is thus striving treats that entity as the foundational basis for the exertion involved in the movement of the sacrificial canopy and the ritual circle.

In this matter, our position is that [the reason] is not invariably concomitant (*pratibaddha*). Therefore, even though the subject at hand is established, logic remains in one's own hands; it is only from outsiders, such as common cowherds, that one appears bewildered.
For who, being diligent, would resort to such a deployment of logic?

By its very own cause, that entity possesses a nature that is closed off to destruction; this is the result of its non-connection with a fixed time. Just as at the moment of the heavy blow of a mallet from one possessing the power of the first lineage, [the pot] abandons its state as a whole and becomes a mass of shards; for even when examined by the eye, one perceives the object named "destruction" [only then]. And thus it is said:
First, this jar is seen; likewise, the falling mallet is seen;
the mass of rags [used as a shield] is seen; but beyond that, no other non-existence is seen.
Where has the scriptural statement "non-existence" been placed, or what is its cause here?
This row of potsherds is merely seen, independent [of any external agent], like a crossbar.

Furthermore, having apprehended the negator—which is unperceived, of the nature of non-cognition, and distinct from [the object]—and without determining even the object of negation (niṣedhya), such as a jar, a cloth, a leaf, or a word, which exists as something other [than the negator], he says: "Because the identity of the negated and the negator is untenable.
For indeed, in the case of destruction, there is no [fragmentation into] millions of shards...

In the case of a jar or a cloth, where there is a birth produced by a destructive cause distinct from the [prior] series of moments (*pālavalaya*), the state of being a negator or the disintegration thereof has been made perceptible; therefore, that which is to be negated must be understood as distinct [from the negation]. Furthermore, since these two have been severed by the cruel saw of critical inquiry, they cannot be identical. Thus, the application of logic, weighing scales, and so forth, does not intrude into one another, for their respective natures are established as observed by the eyes of all people.

If [the world] were pervaded by difference, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total denial of the manifold nature (*vaiśvarūpya*) of the universe, even while its existence is admitted;
for one who accepts the connection with means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how could that very [connection] serve as a sublater when it is the opposite?
All entities are established by their own inherent natures (*svabhāva*) through their respective natures.
Since things participate in exclusions from both their own-nature and other-natures,
therefore, based on whichever exclusions of objects there may be, various distinctions of universals (*jāti*) are conceptualized by those who apprehend their specific differences. (2)

By this logic, indeed, from its own cause, its very nature—which is distinct from another—arises as something imminent in its production; it falls under the sway of the two types of recollective conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) that manifest in accordance with its own self and display the affirmation and negation of objects, both internal and external. Thus, even one possessed of firm pride must accept this consequence. ... Just as sugar, fire, a circle, a bracelet, a joke, and so forth, once placed within the heart, bind everything together through their inherent capacity for conjunction, which depends on the basis of their arising. (4)

— Having dispelled even the notion of a self that extends to the edge of the ocean as something unconfused, by the power of the manifestation of its own nature, if this [cognition] likewise establishes it; then,

having attained a state free from the contact of discordant times, it bears the relationship of a nature delimited by the specific conditions provided by the very causes of things such as the bolt of heaven and the herd of cows, while you, however, are the locus of the burden of a contrary relationship.
Well then, what loss is there for you, O Śubhaśrī? This has now come to pass:
"The existence of things as separate from their own nature is established by their inherent characteristics."
Furthermore, there is great distress in the hearts of opponents regarding what has been accepted [as a reason].

[The term] "destruction" (*vināśa*) is formed by adding the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), according to the rule that it occurs "frequently" (*bahulam*). Thus, it is designated as a "perishing entity" (*vinaśvara-padārtha*) because it arises from a cause of production other than the cause of its own birth.
Intending "destruction" (vināśana) to mean "perishing" (vināśa), he again employs an *asamartha-samāsa* [an ungrammatical compound], stating:

"It is not said that 'existence becomes,' but rather that 'non-existence becomes,'" and so forth; for in this way alone does the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) function, [showing that] "action" is merely the negation of action.
Let this venerable one be so.
"Existence [is that which] has all its causal efficiency (artha-kriyā) destroyed by annihilation"—

thus spoke Vācaspati, the very commentator on the system of Nyāya who should be called the logician of the doctrine of non-existence (anartha-nyāya). Was such a description as this ever intended for you?
Destruction, by the force of its nature as a real entity, is like a door-bolt or like sugar; it is indeed a positive state of being, and thus your [arguments] do not effect anything against it.
Therefore, how could there not be an uninterrupted continuity of activity throughout the three moments,
since its time, like its place and form, is held to be determined by its cause? (2)

If one maintains that destruction consists in the production of annihilation, then in the production of a subsequent destruction, there would be a succession of destructions; thus, that entity could never be fully resolved.
For there is no cessation other than destruction. (3)
If it is argued that there is mutual destruction, how so?
Because in that case, there is the observation of a real entity; thus, it is not the manifestation of a non-existent destruction.

And if it is said that the cessation of the entity called "destruction" occurs because no object is perceived at that time, then [the following applies]: "Destruction is either the very object, such as the mallet, or else the fragments themselves," as stated by the venerable [Śāntarakṣita] in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*. Furthermore, regarding the cessation of that which is to be conventionally designated, its locus in terms of place, time, and form must conform to the requirements of worldly usage for each specific conventional agent.

Since it lies upon the bed of conceptual construction produced by the non-perception (*anupalambha*)—namely, the seeing of that appearance and of another object distinct from it—how could there be any birth for that which is insubstantial? Thus, the effort of [your] dangling words is like fruit growing upon a fruitless tree.
Therefore, you must accept that it is merely the cessation of conventional usage that becomes the object of discourse.
The object is contradicted further, but its production is not; so what is the use of a cause?
If it were due to contradiction alone, why is there no activity toward it at once? Its non-arising is due to the exhaustion of the cause.
Contradiction must be real, for otherwise there would be a destruction of the mutual intrinsic nature of reality.

Therefore, whatever cause possesses its complete nature, when producing its own effect, produces it as adorned with the state of perishability and necessarily limited by time; for its nature is such that it ceases from another [cause], not from the cause of its birth.
Having produced destruction, that cause becomes its destroyer.
If it were to produce that very same perishable state, what would happen?
If it is argued that "if there is no dependence even for a single moment, one entity cannot belong to another entity," [we reply:
indeed, such an entity exists; but how can an entity exist when there is non-existence?

Therefore, the meaning of the proof is: "Whatever effect belongs to a particular causal complex is not distinct from it and is independent [of anything else]. Who indeed would not accept that very property? But what is this "destruction"? It is simply the effect itself. By what logic should one act [toward it]? Is it because the effect is devoid of that [complex]?
Not the first [alternative], for it would follow that the same designation would apply to the auxiliary causes as well.
"Because the nature of separation cannot be defined," and so forth.

Just as one who has acquired undesirable objects and is beset by poverty and the like experiences mental distress through the power of perception, so too does the delightful kingdom of the mind— characterized by the blossoming of the movement of joy in the temple of lethargy—
arise at birth through its own determined temporal nature.

Just as a lotus flower and the like are placed by another who possesses birth, the etymological derivation has already been shown; yet, that very nature of having the property of non-momentary duration arises from its own cause in such a way that one of dull intellect, though seeing it,
does not discern the production of successive similar [moments], being deceived by the constant attachment to the existence of that [object] due to simultaneous perception.
Or [the opponent might argue that] those who perceive the final moment are deceived by their certainties,
because they later fail to perceive its continued existence.
"At the time of determination" means that at that time, impermanence is established.
Even though the capacity to produce an effect is the very nature of the cause, if— (6)— one does not observe its performing that effect [at that time], then...
"...just as one understands a cause from the observation of its effect when that relationship is well-established.

Even though his intention was thus exceedingly clear, radiant, and free from delusion, and even though he had demonstrated it with every means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), Udayana looks upon this [work]— which is marked by an extremely wretched moisture— as his own place of refuge.

If it is argued that when it is said "the cloth has arisen," no one says "the threads have perished"—because the cloth is not something over and above [the threads], and because there is no such conventional usage since there is no perception of difference when only the threads are produced—[we reply: then [your position] is not tenable. If it is further argued that even the basis for conventional usage does not exist in a heterogeneous continuum, [we reply: this is not so. If the cessation of the cloth were merely the threads themselves, then how could the cloth—which is based on them or identical with them—be something entirely different from before? [This is impossible,] just as consciousness cannot be [identical to its material cause].

The difference produced by the individual [manifestation] is perceived, yet that produced by the [underlying] substance has not yet been established; thus, while the meditation on a portion of a cubit’s length within a crystal-shaped monastery is clear, another distinct proficiency—the skill in breaking open the jars joined by its own structural bonds—is also vividly manifest.
In some cases, there is a lack of recognition of this [difference] due to the occurrence of another similar [object].
Because one who does not perceive the difference due to delusion is like [one who perceives] the difference between illusory balls.
For instance, observing a lamp or similar object as it lacks a mark [of continuity], is not joined to what follows, and arises anew, a person indeed determines its destruction.

Thus, even on account of the possibility of perception and non-perception—which serve as the basis for the conventional usage of existence and non-existence—he who is bold with pride exults: "Who else, moreover, is more wise than I, an expert in the ultimate? A discerning person perceives by direct perception the manifestation [of a reflection] when looking at a crystal slab; it is certainly not the case that what is broken is [itself] broken, nor that what is not broken is [itself] broken. (4)

The linguistic usage [expressed as] "possessing [destruction]" is indeed a usage produced by the exclusion of that [destruction] from its true nature; for you have not demonstrated the pervasion of "being produced" by "impermanence" by taking this meaning [of destruction].
Since destruction is invariably concomitant with mere existence, sound is impermanent.
O Agni, if there were no production of something internal, the wood would not be visible;
if it is argued that its very non-destruction constitutes its destruction, how can that be?
Let there be the mutual destruction [of atoms]; why then is the wood not perceived?
If it is argued that this is because of the grasping of those [atoms], no, for by that [grasping] there is no obstruction.
If destruction were itself destructible, then wood would be seen again after its production; for when the killer is slain, Caitra does not come back to life.

And as for the claim that "it is just so": if the killer were not distinct from the non-death [of the wood], then since destruction would be non-different [from the wood], the wood itself would simply perish.

Because it exists, destruction cannot be without a cause; there is no other possible course. Even if destruction were causeless, since it would be eternal, there would be the consequence of its coexistence with the entity; for how could that which is non-existent be eternal? (8)
Furthermore, the consequence that non-existence would be subject to destruction by cultivation is also not tenable.
Since the destruction of an entity is not held to occur through an external destroyer,
but rather the perishing entity itself is independent of anything else,
that [negation] is employed for the purpose of making that known.
The cause of its state has been explained by the mind, having superposed a distinction upon it.
An entity that has come into being is not conceived as being subject to destruction by another state of being;

rather, because it arises spontaneously in such a manner, for the purpose of negating a property that depends on something else, one mentally distinguishes the subject from other factors by making known its own intrinsic nature (*tatsvabhāva*). Then, when there is a desire to know that [nature] alone, the intrinsic nature itself is spoken of in that way.

(2) Thus, those of dull intellect, having seen it in such a manner in certain instances, are deceived by a mere semblance and superimpose upon that entity a quality of destruction. Whether with cause or without cause, they conceive of themselves through the contemplation of the non-existence of that duality as being unestablished.
(3) "If this conceptualization of non-existence occurs even regarding an entity that exists by its own nature, then this [conceptualization] is the same [as before].
Nothing at all happens to that [entity]; it simply does not exist," and so forth.

This [work], though possessing the well-spoken words of the Lord of Logic (*Nyāyanātha*) such as "existence does not become [non-existence]," increases the darkness-like grain of intelligence even within the forest of the wise by means of its own composition— which, though not evil, acts like a layer of *akālakuṭi* weeds— through the verbal analysis of this [text] which is devoid of the investigation of fire.
Nor is there an absence of valid cognition, because those who perceive the final moment have a certain conviction [regarding it].
Since there is a limit [to its duration], it does not arise [as something permanent]; for instance, when one observes the shards and the bracelet, the observer does not perceive a jar.
Indeed, that which does not exist at a particular time is not perceived at that time.

Like a substance transported to another land from a different region, the very description of the cultivation of its own nature— finding refuge in the delightful methods of worldly convention— is repeatedly spoken of as a state entirely dissimilar to the form of non-perception.

This independence, which is proclaimed by the arrangement of the causal factors (*kārakahetu*), is indeed dependent when considered in relation to the indicative cause (*jñāpakahetu*). What, then, does the elder investigator say?

From the threads gathered in the basket of a widow, there are perceived objects designated as "cloth" and the like— possessing the state of being stretched out and woven— which bear a grosser distinction from the weaver’s joy-bestowing hands;
these objects, characterized by specific functions such as serving as garments, are regarded by others as being preeminent in their pride due to the increase in substance.
The word "jar" functions by excluding those causes that produce an effect identical to it, without implying the exclusion of the various specific potencies of form and so forth.

For the word "thread" (*tantu*) is based on actions such as binding; having produced a specific collection of them, its capacity for the purpose of making a cloak or the like must be established by excluding other collections that are not of that nature.
Thus, the word "cloth" (*paṭa*) is revealed by those who seek its meaning.
By means of those threads, the subsequent effect is called "this cloth."
That which arises from the processing of threads is by no means simultaneous;
some [claim this] through the superimposition of the cause,
or even by means of the removal of one [thread].
One should employ the designation "threads" for the effect while demonstrating that the Veda does not depend [on such worldly conventions];

for the cloth is indeed the effect of the threads, and at that time the threads no longer exist. However, the cognition of "threads" arises through the superimposition of the nature of the cause upon the effect, based on the recollection of what preceded.

Because it is dependent [on other factors], or because when each individual [element] is excluded—namely, when each individual thing to be defined is excluded—there is no other "cloth" apart from those names; thus, a temporal distinction whose object is the entire collection of real things must be explained specifically regarding their difference. Otherwise, how could the identity of the referent of recognition be established? Therefore, he remained silent on this point.

Furthermore, through such investigations as whether the destruction of a thread consists in the general absence of the thread or its specific nature, [the opponent] has determined that the very fact of being the cause or non-cause of the essential nature or non-essential nature of the destructible object constitutes a refutation. Thus, fearing—as it were—the manifestation of a distinct entity called "destruction" for every multitude of objects produced by the entire collection of causal factors, and considering that his own previous position regarding the time prior to destruction has not been overturned upon further reflection, he simply stated: "Why is the wood not seen? and so forth, thereby applying the designation "non-existence" to a distinct entity.
or by way of worldly convention,
or by way of the operation of valid cognition.

Whether by the power bestowed through the causal impulse of Maheśvara’s intention, or because entities follow their own inherent tendencies, the meditative absorption (samādhi) known as Sudarśana has everywhere cast down all [other] entities. Why then, like the worship of a thief, should one depart with such frivolous shifting of words and movements—speaking in such a manner as "if that state existed at that time, then its absence has arisen," and so forth? Therefore:
Since destruction is causeless, it follows as a matter of inherent nature;
for among things that depend on other conditions, necessity is not observed.
Even if [the causes] are abundant, there may be non-occurrence of that [effect] in some cases;

for even though the moments exist as the causes of the cause of destruction, because their presence depends upon their own conditions, their presence is not necessarily certain—thus [it is said in the *Mahī*]. (3)

In cases such as the flow of honey, nothing at all is destroyed; for indeed, the lack of ascertainment of a fixed rule is itself the aesthetic charm of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) within the circle of investigation. Therefore, he said:
"By this, variability has been stated, because the effect is not established [as constant]."
Of all those who assert that the cause itself is the destruction of things, who maintain that the cause is the very destruction [of its effect].

Therefore, even at the moment immediately following [the destruction] caused by the impact of a fierce blow from a hammer, fire, or contact with heat, when one observes a transformation into something dissimilar—such as potsherds or embers—the entity, such as a jar or a piece of wood, is seen to have arisen as perishable by its very nature; for that reason, the entity is not perceived [in its original form]. Thus, it is established that perishability, being the nature of destruction, is a pervader of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) because it is independent [of other causes] and is necessarily present. Therefore:
It indeed exists by way of its own nature (*svabhāvataḥ*). Wherever it exists, even elsewhere it exists by way of its own nature.
This very thing, being observed in some place, exists by way of its own nature precisely because of its independence; thus it exists by way of its own nature elsewhere as well.
Because there is no distinction [between the two].

Thus, for one who refutes the stated pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) by raising it in a different form, there is not even satisfaction of his own heart. If it is argued that "pervasion" is therefore "inevitability" (*dhruvabhāvitva*), we say no; because [inevitability] lacks identity with that [the probandum] and lacks its causal nature. (8)
Regarding the phrase "because of being a negation" and so forth:
identity (*tādātmya*) and the possibility of having that same single cause were established immediately prior;
nor does anyone say that because it is an absence (*abhāva*), it is not produced because it lacks the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvatva*).

What then? It is the prattle of fools to claim that non-existence (*abhāva*) is either a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) or an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). Furthermore, as for what kind of non-existence it should be: it cannot be a simple negation, because in that case the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with a verbal action, whereby there would be a mere negation of action; this is known through the operation of a single means of valid cognition and is understood by the power of ignorance.
The notion that knowledge possesses a nature opposed to dependence on another and a nature consisting in the exclusion of [other] entities is a conceptual construction by Jñānaśrīmitra.
Whether established or unestablished, dependence as a relation is an adherence of form; likewise, no other [relation] is ultimately real. (2)

Thus it has been declared in the *Sambandhaparīkṣā*. Therefore, since the remainder of the treatise consists solely of positive injunctions (*vidhi*) that have already been cleared away by [our] intellect, we shall now strive to clear away other treatises as well.
Regarding objects such as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), hair, grass, mud, stalks, and so forth, [it is] like a lamp... (3)

Even though a jar that has been cut and grown back again possesses equal maturity, it does not differ from its former state due to the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the jar and the crystal, because they share the nature of being related entities.

If it is argued that the identity of their intrinsic nature (*samānasvabhāvatva*) is unproven—since the objects [of the two cognitions] are not conflated with contradictory properties, and because even a blind person who connects a jar, a crystal, a bowl, and an earring-ornament (*maṇḍala-maṇḍana*) perceives them as distinct, and thus one [the later] is produced having been separated from the bound [former]—[we reply: no.
This is not the capacity of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Or, if it were established [as a means of valid cognition], there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) based on its substratum;

that fault cannot be averted even by a thousand [other] faults. Furthermore, even if one were to sit for hundreds of aeons, no one is capable of elaborating upon another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) that is consistent with momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), which has already been presented.

Furthermore, even when the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have ceased to function regarding a remote object, a discerning person is not capable of determining its existence. Unity belongs to that which is an undifferentiated cognition; that which is not so [i.e., differentiated] is like something possessing distinction.
If this [means of cognition] were not a proof, it would not be established. (7)
The proof for difference is established [as follows]:
white, suffering, and so forth appear as distinct within the cognition and the feeling, yet they are non-distinct.
If these two—which appear non-distinct—are indeed distinct, then upon what basis could difference and non-difference depend?
Because even those [mental states] that are suppressed by a sharp [consciousness] are seen not to be distinct at times,
the establishment of the distinction between mind and mental factors is proven within the stream of their continuity.

Thus, it is impossible to set aside the words of the Teacher by means of another treatise; for the well-sung and excellently chanted song of the virtuous, which was unattainable, is now obtained as the very breath of the fruit of melodic chanting. (9)
The fruit of your song is such that even the sons of the cowherds sing the Sāman with notes beyond [human] capacity.

By this, the following undesirable [position] is also crushed: "The entity under dispute does not differ even at different times, because it is not associated with contradictory properties (viruddhadharma). Whatever is not associated with contradictory properties even when there is a difference in X, does not differ even when that X differs;
for example, just as a single atom remains one despite the difference between atoms in a continuous series, so too this entity under dispute does not differ even at different times."

Regarding this pervasion (*vyāpti*), no one at all would disagree; since the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) has already been established for you, the stability or instability of entities [is proven]. Because the property of the subject is established, it is not a [separate] means of proof, nor is it something that needs to be proven.

Thus, it has been well established by this treatise that existence—belonging to an entity situated between prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), and occupying the interval between them—is sufficient to demonstrate its permanence; for, when the presence of the probans in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) is established through the culmination of favorable consequences and their contraries, and the necessary connection with the probandum is shown in certain instances such as seeds, this should be firmly grasped by the wise as a most excellent proof. Therefore, we now proceed to strike down the swift-footed [opponent] who leaps lightly over these arguments.

If, for a given thing, a cause of its conventional designation is conceived through its exclusion from others, then the blueness produced therein as that cause of its conventional designation is the "blueness of the conventional designation"; it exists as possessing that conventional designation.

In the case of a lotus, the designation of contradictory properties— namely, performing and not performing [the action of growing] at earlier and later times— is considered the cause for the conventional usage of a difference in seeds, by way of its emerging and delighting [in growth]. Therefore, in this instance, the performance and non-performance are not seized by the fallacy of being unestablished (*asiddha*), because they are observed through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Even when confronted with the multitude of specific objections, its capacity to approach the fault of "inconclusiveness" (anaikāntikatva)— which has already crushed the host of defects through its status as a composition of ancient boldness— is not sustained. For the nature of causality, however slightly it may be considered, must indeed be examined through the discernment of positive and negative concomitance (anyavyatireka).
Because of the investigation of another passage [of the text]:

"This alone is difference, or rather the cause of difference, namely, the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) and its basis in production; and difference consists in the determination of the homogeneity or heterogeneity of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), which is characterized as the cause"—thus it was stated by the venerable Teacher (the Master).

Since this very distinction— which serves as the cause for the conventional usage of the differences between qualities and substances such as direction and time, and between production and destruction— is established as the stable cause for their conventional designation, being a humanly existent reality that is not subject to the expansion of the opponents' arguments regarding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) or non-extension (*avyāpti*), and which acts as the hand pointing out the distinctions of direction, time, and so forth in every instance of perception— then even for those properties superimposed by conceptual construction, the distinction is characterized precisely by the imposition of contradictory attributes (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*). Thus, the charge of "non-pervasion" (*avyāpti*) is impossible.

Since no superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) is ever observed even where there is no difference, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Furthermore, because the cognition of contradiction occurs in many ways and regarding many things, one should not hold in mind the opposite of possibility (*sambhava*).
Nor is there an impossibility of the distinction between two contradictory properties even in that case, for [it exists] eternally.

—By means of the principle of genus (*jāti*), two contradictory entities are excluded; there is no such thing as a "property" (*dharma*) other than this. Rather, although the designations "property" and "possessor of property" (*dharmidharmin*) occur through the exclusion or inclusion of other properties, there is no real difference in the entity itself. Therefore, one should not entertain the notion of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), for this [designation] is possible according to conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). As for what was further stated—that difference (*bheda*) indeed deviates from contradiction (*virodha*)—[that is not so].

The statement that "contradiction does not imply difference" was spoken with reference to the distinction between ultimate and non-ultimate reality. For when the pervasion is established through a connection based on proximity, a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*)—which would favor the similar instance (*sapakṣa*)—is not observed; and this is because the reason serves as the indicator for the conventional usage of difference.
This is a distinction in expression.

There is also a second application: the reflective judgment (*parāmarśa*) "this is that very same [thing]" is an operation consisting of the determination (*dhyavasāna*) of an object as excluded from dissimilar things. For example, when a mass of hair has been cut and regrown, there is the reflective judgment "this is that very same [hair]"; likewise, in the case of a jar or similar object which is extremely similar [to its prior state], there is the judgment "this is that very same [jar]"; and in the case of something with slight similarity, there is the judgment "this is like that," according to the context.

—Regarding this, it has been stated here that when there is identity of birth (*jātyekatva*), as in the case of a lamp and so forth, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is explained as having the exclusion of others (*tadvyāvṛtti*) as its object.
If there were no identity whatsoever between the past and the present, how could there be the performance of a causal function (*arthakriyā*) seen previously and subsequently? [Objection: No;

just as one observes a single jar being used for the purpose of placing a sprout in a broken jar, and just as there is the carrying of a city (or a load), so too is there conformity with the prior state.

Since such causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) will occur even in the absence [of a single entity], and since that unity— which consists in the exclusion of what does not perform that specific causal efficiency— is accepted as merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) due to its performance of that single causal efficiency, the argument that "the momentary destruction of jars and so forth is established by those very same proving reasons" is refuted.
For designations and conceptual constructions such as "one" are based solely on the capacity of their respective objects— (3)

—By this [reasoning], those conceptualizations (*vyapadeśavikalpa*) that take as their object a commonality of purpose (*arthasāmānya*) based on a similarity of purpose are not respected by discerning people, even if they arise from a similar class such as the *samaṅgī* plant. Therefore, unity (*ekatva*) is the object of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) precisely because of its capacity for such causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Consequently, whatever recognition there is, it has as its object a thing capable of a similar causal efficiency, distinguished from other things that do not perform that specific causal efficiency; just as when one intends to bring a jar, but upon being commanded "bring another," one brings a different jar.

"This is that very same [object] which was brought here" is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). And if this recognition—"This is that very same jar"—were to arise as a manifestation persisting from birth until destruction, it would follow that there is momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) at every instant; for such [recognition] would belong to an entity [only if it were permanent]. (6)

And there is a subverting proof against the contrary: the manifestation of a thing situated between prior non-existence and posterior non-existence is, in reality, transcendent to the limitations of preceding and succeeding time.
That which has transcended [temporal] determination is the ground of experience for all things and for virtuous people.

Therefore, even the temporal restriction of entities is established within their most substantial nature (*sthavīyasī svabhāva*). However, the conceptual determination of oneness—which has as its object the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of what is not that nature—does not entail the existence of a state [of identity]; rather, it is the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that operates with a conventional oneness for the sake of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

By removing the delusion of others, even regarding a negation that is accessible to cowherds and the like through the power of the non-perception of what is visible, the *Vyāmohaśuddhitant*ra is introduced, targeting their doubts; [it is said]:
"For the sake of those who are utterly deluded, because it is not within the conventional experience of cowherds and the like."
Because of this statement:
"But dhyāna, by means of the manifestation of the object, is said to reveal it; thus, even in its absence, [the result] is produced by it."

Likewise, in cases such as fine linen, blue lotus petals, rows of folds, women who delight the heart, jasmine, vermilion, and the tops of roof-ridges, it is stated that a single synthesizer (*pratisaṃdhātṛ*) appears here all at once, by virtue of a subsequent reflective awareness (*pāścātyānuvyavasāya*) which conceals the perception of the apprehended forms known as their intermediate states.

The "vibration" (*sphuraṇa*) is the manifestation of the previously experienced form of the grasper (*grāhakākāra*) by virtue of a single reflective awareness (*ekavimarśa*) that is turned away from what is not that [form];

and the "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) and so forth are established through the form of the real entity (*vastustoma*) which is turned away from the imagined nature (*parikalpitarūpa*), arranged in a manner conducive to momentary destruction. Therefore, one should attend with a discerning mind that there is no defect of doubt in any respect regarding the proof of impermanence (*anityatāsādhana*). Thus—
Furthermore, even an object such as a diamond or a sapphire would be permanent because it is independent of anything else; consequently,
it would simultaneously produce cognitions of everything in the world at once.
"Those [causes] become its successive [effects] through the assistance of cooperative conditions;
they say there is a difference at every moment. Here too, as before, the fault is present. (4) Passages such as this should also be introduced as appropriate, having cast aside all fear.

Furthermore, as for the claim that no designation whatsoever occurs without substances, qualities, actions, and so forth—including time—and that there can be no speech without such designations, and therefore time and the rest exist by virtue of speech alone, which establishes their momentariness—that too is refuted.
Time has as its inferential mark the cognitions of priority and posteriority, simultaneity and non-simultaneity, slowness and quickness, with respect to their respective objects. (9)

Because no other cause is possible for the arising of things that are distinct from their prior conditions, that which serves as the cause here is time (*kāla*). Where there is a posterior condition relative to space (*dig*), there alone is the anterior condition produced by time; and where there is an anterior condition relative to space, there alone is the posterior condition produced by time. This intermixture and conjunction is what constitutes [the nature of] time.
"These were done simultaneously and these were done sequentially;

it was done long ago and it was done quickly"—such [notions] do not constitute perception of time as something distinct from form and the other [sensory objects], for slowness is merely a contradiction arising from the sequence of causes in the production [of an effect].
Furthermore, succession belongs only to an entity through its presence and absence; time is not [itself] an entity, just as in the expression "the head of a rabbit. Again— (9)
The designation "this is the time of the entity" is established as follows:
"the state of having been seen is the past; the state of being seen is the present; and the state of being about to be seen is the future. Thus is the determination.

Form (*rūpa*) is also to be understood as being produced by the eye-consciousness, and likewise sound and the other [objects] are to be understood as being based on their respective sense-faculties and causes.

The establishment of substantial entities (*dravya*) has also been shown to be achieved through the exclusion of causes and effects that are established by their respective aggregates; thus, there is no conventional usage which is not invariably connected with impermanence within this position.
In the *Vādarahasya*, the second chapter is the *Nirṇaya* (Determination) of the *Nyāya* which establishes the existence of the referent through exclusion;
the third chapter is the *Apoha-pratyūha-vyūha-nirāsa* (Refutation of the Array of Objections against Apoha).
Here, the array of obstacles regarding exclusion (*apoha*) is dispelled.

In this world, for a living being who is awake, immediately following the diffusion of the eye toward a mass of blue, vast, moving, and perceivable objects such as a crest of hair, two things are determined: first, a manifestation grounded in the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of blue and so forth; and second, a manifestation of blue and so forth that is bound to a non-common cognition through the subsequent mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*). Both of these are repeatedly observed to be unimpaired and capable of determining blue and the like.

For cognitions possess the power of delimitation, and both of these possess the appearance of blue, which is the basis for the determination of blue; therefore, the common worldly person’s conviction is that both, having escaped from fear, delimit nothing other than the blue itself.

However, the commentator [Dharmakīrti], relying on an unbridled reasoning regarding the nature of reality (*tattva*), first stated that perception is "non-conceptual" (*avyapadeśya*) and "of a determinate nature" (*vyavasāyātmaka*).
This non-conceptual [perception] is indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*), resembling the cognition of infants, the mute, and so forth;

thereafter, that cognition by which an object is subsequently determined through its properties such as genus (*jāti*) and the like is also accepted as being perceptual—thus [he treats it as] conceptual (*savikalpaka*).
The sense of sight (*kṣa*) shines forth in the discernment of objects such as lotuses when conjoined with [factors] like genus;

however, the Buddhist has determined that the first [moment] alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while the second is for the purpose of verbalizing through the causal complex of recollection, mental application, and so forth. (7)
It arises from the completeness of the eye and other [causes].

Rather, it is accepted as being unestablished [as a direct perception] because it arises from the aspect grasped by a cognition characterized by a middle state, accompanied by recollection, mental application (*ābhoga*), and so forth;

furthermore, the basis for its determination here is the appearance of blue and so on, which has been transferred from the recollection of the blue eye, even when the object—the eye and the blue color—is absent.
From what could it arise?
Not from an object, because that has already ceased;
nor from water and so forth, because those have the nature of being pervaded by form and other qualities.
For this has been said:
"And that [cognition], following along with the general cognition (*sāmānyavijñāna*), is not perceived;
by whom was that slight trace of the form of blue and so forth produced within it?"

Just as the cognition arising from words is observed to be the same whether [the object] has perished or not, such is the case for things that exist; this is not so for cognitions of the ear and other senses.
Thus,
even that inclusive cognition which appears as the manifestation of a word and individual [object] is described as "cowness" (gotva),
for it is devoid of the forms of color, shape, and syllables.
The nature of substance and so forth consists of form and the like;

however, this conceptual [cognition], which has the aspect of letters and the configuration of blue and so forth, is well known to be manifested as the internal experience of the "mere-internal" (*mātra*) and other states.

Therefore, there is no pride of delimiting [the object] as genus and so forth for the second cognition, because its nature is the opposite of that [first cognition], due to its being of the nature of form (*rūpa*).
For where the appearance of something is impossible, that [cognition] cannot be the apprehender of it;
just as the cognition of form, though empty of the aspect of touch, does not apprehend touch.
In the same way, this [cognition] which appears as blue and so forth is established as not being a cognizer of universals (*jāti*) and the like that are empty of that intrinsic nature;
for it is merely a transformation (*vivarta*) of that other [object], namely, sensation (*vedanā*).
"The established position that exclusion (apoha) is manifested by both word and logical mark is being set forth in order to establish the fact that all phenomena are inexpressible";
thus, its status as a thesis is restated.
The secret here, moreover, is this: by that very cognition through which blue is determined as the exclusion of the non-blue, one's own status as having exclusion as its object is not established;
what then?

Because this appearance is distinct from its own moment of blue due to being sublated by another cognition, even those who compose the most advanced treatises speak of it with respect to that cognition. Furthermore, the non-establishment of momentariness for that which is perceived by mental contact is not applicable here, because conventional usage is established otherwise; for words, logical marks, and conceptual constructions are common [to both].
It is undisputed that those who do not establish the form [of an object] are incapable of even bending a blade of grass,
because they lack a stable or unstable investigation regarding the existence of external objects;
and that [form] is false.
There are three positions: [the cognition consists of] the mental aspect (*ākāra*), or the external object, or both.
Among these, it is not the first position; for that [aspect] must be established as such based solely on experience, yet it is not apprehended because it is unreal.
Or, if that were the case, it would contradict [the nature of] purposeful activity;
for even after experiencing "this is unreal," one who seeks causal efficacy does not engage [with it].
If it is argued that this fault does not apply because there is the manifestation of the exclusion of other [objects], [we reply:]...
This very [absence] is non-existent, because there is only the manifestation of that which has a positive form (vidhirūpa).
For here, through word or logical mark, there is no manifestation such as "there is no non-fire in this location of the mountain," but rather "fire exists.
Even if one were to say, "I perceive a cessation," and so forth.
Because here, on this earth which supports the mountains, fire exists; and since consciousness assumes the form of Agni (Dhanañjaya), by that very consciousness Agni himself is cognized.
Therefore, it is entirely our own view that this is due to the recollection of the Creator (Vidhi) alone.
However, it is called "false" (alīka) because of the statement: "In the world, that which does not possess luminosity and is sublated is called false."
That which is being manifested is said to be sublated.

Why, then, is it said that "not by that very experience," and so forth? Even setting aside the linguistic expression for a moment, for the proponent of formlessness (*nirākāravādin*), [the object] is indeed cut down by the wheel of analysis into the one and the many, just like a material substance.

The mind itself, appearing in the form of blue and so forth, is called a false wheel; yet this [designation] does not arise from the power of its own self-experience, but rather depends upon a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-bodha*).
Likewise, the very internal mind (*svānta*) when pervaded by the form of a blue lotus is said to be the "exclusion of the non-blue" (*anīla-vyāvṛtti*).

If the exclusion of blue were something distinct [from blue], then blue, by being excluded from that [distinct entity], would merge with non-blue itself, just like non-blue; moreover, in that case as well, there would be an exclusion of another and a thing excluded from another.
And sounds, as well as immovable things, conform to their respective causes.
The two [terms], which respectively exclude or do not exclude other differences,
are the basis for the distinction of linguistic convention, in accordance with the desire of the cognizer.

In that case as well, if the meaning of a word were the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), then the exclusion would be something entirely different from the excluded; for if the excluded were to cease by means of an exclusion that is distinct from itself, it would follow that the excluded entity itself does not exist. And thus, there would be no engagement with it either. Therefore, that which is excluded is itself the basis for the application of the word "excluded. Furthermore, while there is a distinction in the application of words, this distinction arises from a difference in convention and a difference in the denotable object. But surely, since there is no difference in the denotable object, a difference in convention is also untenable; for [in the view of] the two [parties], there is only one...
Because of this movement, there is likewise no employment of a case-ending that implies distinction (*vyatirekin*), since such a suffix is based on difference.
Even when two things are denoted by a single word,
the distinct case-ending follows as if the meaning were different, due to a slight particularity in what is expressed.

Indeed, the operation of a word with respect to its object does not depend on the inherent nature of that object; for if it did, it would follow that no such operation could occur. Therefore, whether [the word] is intended to be used as denoting something distinct or non-distinct, it reveals that object without obstruction once it is released from [its own form].
Thus, "cow, cow" (gauḥ, gauḥ).

Even when the single referent "you" (*tvam*) is denoted, it is contradicted by the cognition of a certain specific quality; thus, due to a difference in convention, the case-ending, although its meaning is not distinct [from the stem], appears as if indicating a different object,
because of the habitual observation of such usage even where there is no difference in meaning.
There is no differentiation [of the word] everywhere, because even elsewhere—just as in the case of the word "puruṣa"—there is an absence of such a restrictive connection (*pratibandha*).

Just as a single thing is expressed by this [word] in some instances and in one place, so too, despite the lack of distinction [in the object], there would be no difference in convention (*saṃketabheda*) due to the absence of usage in the plural for the sake of expressing qualities such as "bullishness" (*gaurava*) and so forth; rather, it would be [the same] for another [instance].

For instance, if the meaning of what has been stated is such that this cognizer, without regard for the existence of the exclusion of anything other than that, desires to know merely the exclusion of "horse" regarding a particular individual (*piṇḍa*), then he is informed by a word associated with a convention for that specific exclusion, namely, "this possesses non-horseness. Furthermore, when he is free from any desire for the exclusion of other [exclusions], that [cognition]— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)

When one desires to exclude that very exclusion of "horse" (the horse-exclusion) which has not been previously abandoned, the word is released for the sake of manifesting it as "this is not a non-horse. For this very reason, because the operation of the word in the former case rests upon a different established term, there is neither grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) nor the status of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣyabhāva*), as in "this cow's whiteness," because the cognition— being based on that [exclusion]—
does not appear as a unity due to the distinction of that [quality] alone.
Furthermore, because it is free from further expectancy, it does not apply to a second [object].

Likewise, through the linguistic usage of convention, in that which possesses the property of excluding all conventional designations, there is a manifestation of a single [entity] to many people as if it were divided; and because there is an expectancy for another exclusion, this very distinction exists everywhere between those terms that denote a substance and those that denote an existence.
There is no distinction whatsoever between those two words in their denotable meaning.

Therefore, there is no distinction whatsoever between words expressing a property-bearer (*dharmin*) and its property (*dharma*) based on a contradiction in the determinate cognition regarding the object denoted; for one [word] conveys that very [object] while excluding other distinctions,
whereas another does so without such exclusion— this is the distinction.
Whether one intends to make that meaning known by means of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), or by a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*),
or by some other means, if one should express it, there is no difference [in the meaning] other than that.

And it is only by showing such a distinction that cognition arises as "purity" through that [word], or as "cook-ness" (*pācakatva*) in the case of "cook" (*pācaka*). Or when one asks, "When will he cook?"—it is not by some other convention (*samaya*) created by oneself for the sake of making known such a state, nor does this become a different object merely by being designated as such;
rather, it is precisely that which exists in such a state which is cognized.
—because the convention for the word has been established for the sake of [denoting] that [quality].
Nor is it said "the state of being a cook" (*pācakatva*) in that way;
for here, it is not as if some other person distinct from the act of cooking is designated by the name "cook," such that the act of cooking would be considered separately.
Furthermore, as for that which is its denotation, someone might say it is like "you" even in the sense of being a "cook.

However, there is no single composite [entity] arising from this; and even if there were multiplicity, as before, there would be no movement because of the lack of distinction and because of atomicity.
If it is not established [that atoms are perceived], then there is no distinction; since specific things possess sensory perceptibility, they are therefore not atomic.
By this, the absence of obstruction and other such qualities is also refuted.

In the same way, the forms of number, conjunction, action, and so forth do not appear to the intellect as distinct entities, either by way of their own intrinsic nature or through verbal expression. (8)
It is not reasonable to ask how the obstruction of atoms is perceived given their lack of contact;

for nowhere has anything common to the negation of a composite whole been perceived, such that [obstruction] would not exist in atoms even in the absence of such a reality. Furthermore, [there are other qualities], such as resistance (pratighāta), and so forth. Now, if...
If atoms were variegated in nature, then cloth and other such objects would be produced from their aggregation;
how then could they provide obstruction to sunlight or water?

(10) And how could there be [an object] among atoms, even without a scripture [stating it], consisting of parts whose mutual intermediate spaces are unobstructed? Or rather, it is said here that because of their being an obstruction, [the whole] is produced;

yet how can non-conjoined [parts] produce a whole, since conjunction does not occur simultaneously—otherwise, there would be the consequence of a mass the size of a single atom due to the absence of [any spatial extension beyond] its own nature.

If it is argued that [the atoms] produce conjunction as a distinct category (padārtha), then the same undesirable consequence follows: how can those [atoms] which possess intervals produce that very conjunction?
Furthermore, if it is a mere contact (saṃsarga), what is the need for a separate conjunction? Or is it not so?
Now, if they produce conjunction and a whole while still being separated by intervals, then why do they not also produce effects such as obstruction?
Even without the mutual contact of atoms, there would be a further aggregation; and even upon impact, they would remain distinct entities. (3)
In which [state] that very thing does not exist at all.
Indeed, conjunction does not appear as something distinct from the conjoined objects; rather,

only that state of two things being unjoined is perceived, and when those two are subsequently perceived [as joined], the conclusion is reached through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that this [conjunction] is a mere conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*).

Since you have no direct perception [of the process], your cognition that "it has become such-and-such" or "it has arisen in this way" is merely that very state being made known as a distinct entity called "conjunction. For this very reason:
"In the cognition of a word, by means of conceptual construction which follows after the differentiation of entities..."
Just as in the case of qualities and so forth, it is likewise [impossible] with respect to an object that is merely conceptualized, or one that has perished or not yet been born.
The distinction between word-meanings does not arise merely from a difference in verbal cognition; rather, it arises from a difference in the cognition that characterizes perception.
For conceptual cognition, arising through the power of beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), fluctuates in various ways and thus fails to find firm footing in the reality of the object.

Likewise, cognitions of conjunction and so forth rely on distinctions imagined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Furthermore, the distinction between imagined objects arises even from the views of other non-Buddhist schools (*tīrthya-antaram*), because it is the production of only the imagined that occurs.
Furthermore, there would be an infinite regress in establishing the reality of the object;
by accepting [the need for further proofs] in that manner, there would be mutual contradiction.

Consequently, the distinct word and the cognition arise with respect to a conceptualized object through the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). Of what nature is this conceptualization?

It follows the differentiation of objects. The differentiation of objects is their exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from that which is not as it is; there is no exclusion other than the excluded itself. Therefore, that very [exclusion], in relation to the continuum, appears as a distinction from other things by way of difference, following the differentiation of the objects.
Furthermore, conceptual constructions are understood to follow distinctions [of number],
such as "one quality," "one inherence," or "twenty-four qualities. If there is a metaphorical designation here, one must consider on what basis it is intended.
Why is that very same [nature] not accepted as the cause of both of those in all entities?

Just as in the expression "unborn sons distress their grandfather," let that very basis for the metaphorical designation (upacāra) regarding the past and the unborn— which is grasped through determination and recollection— be the cause even in the case of the present, such as in the expression "the jar is conjoined" and so forth.
If figurative usage does not apply everywhere because the qualifier is distinct,
then from what [source] is it established that the primary meaning applies when there is no distinction, given that the referent is distinct?
Even if they have no other object as their cause, words such as "white" and so forth are not synonyms;
for if even there, words associated with number and the like were to have a different object, [they would still not be synonyms].
There would be no distinction between quality and substance, even though they are different due to a difference in their exclusion (vyāvṛtti),
just as in the case of the words "non-action" and "non-substance" [which differ despite both being negative].
Now, metaphorical designation (upacāra) is indeed dependent upon a primary sense; how could it occur when the primary sense is absent?
And the primary sense is that which possesses a distinct qualifier, as in the case of "the man with the staff" (daṇḍin).

In your view, however, since the status of being primary would exist in some cases due to the absence of distinct qualifiers—because the qualifiers are produced by successive prior conceptualizations—the possibility of metaphorical designation is not established.
That which has a distinct qualifier is indeed primary;

even that which has an undistinct qualifier is considered primary because it has attained conventional usage through extreme habituation, despite its qualifiers being distinguished by conceptual construction.

The unerring activity of cognition always exists in both primary and metaphorical senses, as in the case of "lion" [applied to a man] or "boy"; likewise, there is also a worldly convention [regarding this].
Because of this statement:
since the primary [meaning] of a word is the object of a cognition of unerring movement (*askhalad-gati*), while any other is secondary (*gauṇa*), why is it not sufficient?
If there is a distinction—(8)
—Furthermore, there would be no qualified object; thus, in every case, only the qualified [substance] would be denotable.

In that case, synonymy would result from non-difference in meaning, and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would arise from non-difference in form. For coreferentiality occurs when there is a difference in objective referents; however, cognitions themselves, arising in accordance with their own internal dispositions, construct the linguistic conventions of difference, non-difference, and coreferentiality. Thus, there is no undesirable consequence of synonymy. Even when there is no difference in the object, non-synonyms are observed, such as "non-object" (*akarma*) and "substance" (*dravya*).
Expressions such as "action is devoid of substance" (adravyaṃ karma) and so forth—

therein, is the basis merely a difference in exclusion (vyāvṛttibheda), and not another difference in the ground for application (pravṛttinimittabheda), as in the cases of "cow," "white," "cow," and "cowness"? Furthermore,
that which is indicated by words denoting entities (bhāva) appears as if it were distinct [from the substrate].
By means of words such as "number" and so forth, which denote both the quality and its possessor, there is a differentiation from other properties belonging to that same object.
For one who desires to know only that [specific object], the scripture— without implying all other things—
describes it as if it were a distinct property, like a finger pointing toward something at a certain place.
The term *yuktāṅguli* (joined fingers) denotes the substratum (*dharmin*) for all [fingers] through its application to the eyes;
likewise, even when expressing a single well-known object, it maintains that established configuration.
The term "cow" refers to the entire object as associated with a single, uniform conceptual apprehension;

the term "white," however, refers to a specific part of that [object] which is associated with a different conceptual apprehension, and which exists as a distinction excluded from others through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Therefore, for him, the expression "the cow's white quality" involves a case-ending of distinction (vyatireka-vibhakti), just as in the cases "the body of a stone statue" or "the head of Rāhu. And when there is no apprehension of the form of the cow, only whiteness itself is perceived,
devoid of any specific related entity.

Then one asks, "To what does this whiteness belong? At that time, having ascertained the nature of the cow through previous observation, one points it out, saying, "It is a cow. Thus, identity (*tādātmya*) alone is intended as the relationship here; however, the distinction (*vyatireka*) is [only] conceptualized because of the initial determination of the dominant [perceiver]. But when this [whiteness] must exist by itself—be it due to the dullness of the perception of specific features for those with weak vision—it nevertheless [remains distinct] from other cows by means of this whiteness.
He asks, "It must be known:

what is this? Is it a white cow or something else? At that time, the reply is, "It is a cow. This is because the question itself exists only through its inclusion within that [reply] by virtue of being in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
A response corresponding to that would be mute, and this is the true meaning:
when the certainty of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*),
even if there is some cause for the absence of a specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
This Śakla, being wise, gave this reply to the horse: because the question was characterized by a distinction, there was certainty (the definitive conclusion) that it was "just so";
however, when there is no distinction and it is included within the specific detail, [the same applies].
