Having considered the conduct of the authoritative means of knowledge, the questioner's inquiry should take place.

At that time, one who has not recognized its true nature would give an answer of the same kind; however, there is no possibility of an occasion here for another method [of proof]. Having observed the difference through direct perception, there is no further determination of that difference.
The impossibility of non-difference is not considered the root of inference;
rather, when positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) are established as beginningless,
then because difference exists, linguistic convention proceeds in that very same way.

This beginningless conventional usage has likewise proceeded from old age; however, because the world does not engage in the investigation of the reality of things, its distinction is not sublated. Even so, in the absence of a substance, [there is no] pot.
It might be argued that "form" (rūpa) would be like saying "the form of form," because there is nothing distinct from it; however, this is not so.
The word "jar" excludes those things which have causes and results identical to its own, and it expresses itself by not implying the various specific potencies such as color-form (rūpa) and the rest.
Therefore, there is no scriptural expression of a single substratum such as "the form is the pot. Such a distinction exists between that which denotes a genus and that which denotes a collection.

In the expression "the color and so forth of the jar," because the general property [of "jar-ness"] is subordinate, the specific differences in its capacities are made known; by this same method, other things to be expressed may also be understood.

Is it not the case that in compounds (samāsa), primary derivatives (kṛt), and secondary derivatives (taddhita), there is an expression of a relation (*sambandha*), except in cases of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), where the form is non-differentiated and the relation is invariable?
For example, in *rājapuruṣatvam*, *kārakatvam*, and *aupagavatvam*, the relations are respectively those of owner and owned, action and agent, and offspring and progenitor.
The exception to this is as follows:

(5) from a compound, [the cognition of] "black-serpent-ness" arises through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*); from a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), [the cognition of] "elephant-ness" arises through having performed battle. In these cases, only the genus (*jāti*) is expressed, not the relationship. Furthermore, "whiteness" is expressed by a secondary derivative that does not differ in form from its base; even when ending in a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*), it has a form identical to its base.
In this case as well, only a quality (*guṇa*) is denoted.

A word ending in a *kṛt* suffix has an invariable relation (*avyabhicaritasambandha*); since the category of "being" (*sattā*) is not absent from the referent (*padārtha*), that very relation is what is expressed, according to the principle of verbal cognition (*śābdanyāya*).

If it is asked how the agent (*pācaka*) and the state of being an agent (*pācakatva*) can have the same referent, we reply: no, because the inherence (*samavāya*) of the action [in the agent] has been refuted.

Since identity remains unimpaired even when a distinction is created by conceptual construction, what indeed is untenable? For exclusion and the word excluded have a single referent; thus, regarding the object of *anyāpoha*, the position that it possesses [the universal] has been cut away.
"In the case of separate [entities], there would be a fault because of the production and destruction of that [universal] (*jāti*).
This means that because it is not independent, [the universal] is destroyed by that [destruction of the substance].
The meaning of this is as follows: in this way, the word "existent" (*sat*) denotes a substance (*dravya*) which has the mere nature of the universal (*jāti*) as its subordinate element.
"Not directly" means that it does not imply the specific differences such as a jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth belonging to that [universal].

If that [universal] were not distinct from those [particulars], there would be an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); for where there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is no coreferentiality.
For example, by the word "white," its own denoted quality—(10)

Because it denotes a substance qualified by its measure (*mātra*), there is no implication (*ākṣepa*) of substances such as sweetness even when they exist; consequently, those [qualities] are not its particulars (*bheda*). This same consequence applies elsewhere as well.

It has been stated that for a word, both the universal (*jāti*) and its own form (*svarūpa*) have the substance as their subordinate (*upasarjana*); however, the particularity of the jar and so forth is not like that, because it is separated from both by an interval, and thus possesses dependence (*pāratantrya*). Therefore, it does not imply "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and the like.
And because of its connection with "pot-ness," the pot becomes the locus of existence (*sattā*).

Just as by the word "color" (*rūpa*), there is a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "sweetness" and so forth—which are not implied by it—such as in the expression "white water," so too that objection regarding the formulation of the thesis (*pakṣopavandana*) has been refuted; thus [it is said] in the words of the Teacher (*ācārya*).
And this is also current in the commentary of the Bhāṣyakāra:
"How could this person, whose mind is properly directed, have acted out of the wonder of improper reflection?
Furthermore, even when there is only the appearance of cessation (*nivṛtti*), activity (*pravṛtti*) is not possible."

For one who desires a jar does not act on the grounds that "a non-jar does not exist," but rather on the grounds that "a jar exists" and so forth; because the negation of the other—namely, "a non-jar does not exist"—and the statement "the jar exists," or "something other than a non-jar exists here," or "that which is excluded from what is characterized as a non-jar," all have one and the same meaning. This is because it is only when the intellect is awakened by the sound of the jar's form being fashioned, yet remains unestablished in any particular jar, that the exclusion of the non-jar is determined to be the cause for its engagement with the jar.
It delimits that [object], thereby excludes what is other than it, and indicates the absence of a third possibility; thus, this is the operation of a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If it is argued that there is no such fault because the cognition "only the non-pot is excluded" occurs, [we reply] that as long as the exclusion of the pot is not rejected, the restriction itself remains unestablished.

But what other positive injunction (*vidhi*) could there be for its inclusion [in the cognition], since the very rejection of a negation constitutes a positive injunction? Thus, that which was intended has indeed been illuminated; for it is precisely from the manifestation of the jar’s similarity [to other jars] that the exclusion of everything else occurs.

It has already been stated that this is because it consists in the non-apprehension of that [object]. Thus, according to some, there is first a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*), and subsequently, based on that which arises at a later time, there is the conceptualization of its unreality.

Furthermore, as for what is said: "If it is argued that the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is simply a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*), and that it is a positive entity (*vidhi*) because it has the form of being excluded from others—[we reply: no, because in the case of the theory of unreality (*alīka-pakṣa*), such a thing does not exist; for it would follow that its establishment of its own essential nature would be unreal."

"The [objection] that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not ascend into conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—that too has been refuted by this very [argument]: (9) Through the manifestation of the similarity to a jar, there is the exclusion of non-jars; the affirmation of a gross foundational entity is indeed clearly apprehended by the intellect. Even if it subsequently perishes due to a sublater (*bādhaka*), what fault is there in the initial cognition?

Furthermore, your statement that "the particular characteristic does not ascend into conceptual construction" is not tenable, for in relation to a vivid perception established as the form of a jar excluded from both similar and dissimilar classes, the object is called the particular characteristic."

That very conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), by delineating the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from things of a different class (*vijātīya*), is called a conceptualization through its determination (*adhyavasāya*) of a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) due to its similarity with that [exclusion]. Yet even that [conceptualization] is gross; for no category such as "universal" (*jāti*) is perceived apart from the contact with the nature of the coarse root [of the object], and as for difference, a jar or the like is determined in this very way only at the present moment.
Having intended this meaning, it is said that "in conceptual construction, this particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) appears as excluded [from others].
Since that which is excluded from both [the similar and the dissimilar] necessarily has an exclusion even from one side, it is not said that "the lotus is not non-blue.
And so it has been stated:
That which is the opposite of what has been described is called the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
That universal (sāmānya), moreover, is of three kinds, based on existence, non-existence, and both.

If cognition were dependent upon entities, and an entity [existed] in accordance with [the cognition of] entities, this is not so; for the answer has already been stated, because it is observed [otherwise],
and because it is otherwise in the case of the past and so forth.

If it is argued that there would be a loss of its status as a real entity (bhāva) because that cognition is preceded by the apprehension of an entity, this is not a fault; for the object of cognition (meyam) is indeed the single particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa).
Because it is understood through both its own form and that of another, it is held that there are two objects of cognition (*prameya*).

Furthermore, how can even a positive entity (*vidhi*) not be dependent, since it depends on a nature that is excluded (*vyavacchinna-svabhāva*) in order to possess the character of being a non-positive entity (*avidhi-dharmatva*) within its own positive form?

Therefore, the fact that Jñānaśrīmitra attempted to avoid the charge of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) by shifting it onto linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) during the process of comprehension is merely a means to delude the vulgar, like a wooden ball.

Regarding the objection against the venerable teachers that there is a "shifting of the locus" (*sthānāntarasañcāra*), it is not possible; for we accept precisely the manifestation of the positive injunction (*vidhi*). And that injunction, being cognized from the word, follows convention (*saṃketa*);

yet convention does not apply to an object that has not been previously perceived. Therefore, how can the fault of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*) be avoided by shifting the locus during the formation of the convention? As it has been said: "In the apprehension of the meaning of 'tree' through the exclusion of non-trees, there are two [factors]."
In the absence of the apprehension of a single entity as "this is different from that," there is no apprehension of duality.
"Therefore, some proclaim that the convention is impossible;
for them, are non-trees excluded within the convention or not?"

How can exclusions (vyavacchinna) be known prior to the apprehension of the tree? For if they are not excluded, there would be no conventional usage for those engaged in linguistic practice regarding the designation (saṃketa).
There would be no engagement [with the object] by way of excluding that [other], as in the case of a location containing trees;
for one does not act by merely negating another without having enjoined [the target] or having pointed out a single thing standing before one.
If it is argued that the convention "this is a tree" is established and understood,
and therefore there is no fault even in worldly usage regarding the term "tree," [we reply: no.
The undesirable consequence that "this too is likewise" does not cease;
for [the universal] resides in a single cognition known as the unifying reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*).
Having entered [into that state], one distinguishes for oneself those objects which are causes and those which are not;
these entities, residing within that cognition, appear to the intellect as being its causes.
The statement "one should perceive [things] as distinct, like various forms that are themselves devoid of causal form," is intended to establish distinction.

This very nectar of the supreme well-spoken word has been ground again and again by you as "well said" (sādhu). Furthermore, that which was uttered from the wealth of causes such as the meeting [of conditions], though appearing like a terrifying fragment of doubt, is called "unreal" (alīka) if it is pierced [through analysis].
If this is so— [3] —then what?
Not so, because there is a contradiction.
For "something" is the meaning of a positive injunction (*vidhi*), whereas "nothing" is the meaning of the false (*alīka*).

If falsity were established merely by the exclusion of what does not have that form, it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) would be false.
Even so, who could touch it?

For there is no determination according to reality, and because there is no determination, it is not reality. This conventional [perception] is indeed different from the rule of the manifestation of direct perception.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of existence (*vidhi*). The ultimate (*pāramārthika*) is that thing whose presence or absence causes a difference in the manifestation of cognition; this is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the unique reality (*asādhāraṇa-tattva*), which is the real entity (*vastu*). That alone is ultimately existent (*paramārthasat*), because an entity is defined by its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*).
The other, which is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), is the object of inference; this is the distinction between the apprehended object (*grāhya-viṣaya*) and [the determined object].

However, as for the distinction between the determined object (*adhyavaseya-viṣaya*), it consists of horizontal and vertical universals (*tiryag-ūrdhvatā*). That which is useful therein has the nature of a jar or the like, excluded from what is not that form; it is called a "particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*) because it is excluded from one side, like a blue lotus.
It is not a non-entity, because it is established as being exactly thus.
If there is no establishment of anything else apart from that, it is because that very thing is already established.
The second type of error is held to be due to an improper mental engagement (*ayathābhiniveśa*);
if there were movement by means of another's form, there would be no validity for that error.
The validity of even an erroneous cognition arises from its non-contradiction with the intended object;
furthermore, movement is observed to be otherwise, and this position has already been addressed in another context.

In the conceptualization of what is perceived, only the jar itself manifests—clearly in one case and indistinctly in the other—and the qualified object does not become divided merely by the difference in its qualifiers.

Therefore, in both cases, it is the jar alone that [is the object]; thus, Master Udayana explains that the engagement in linguistic convention proceeds by unifying the perceived object and the conceptualized object.

Consequently, commentators compose various accounts regarding whether [the object] is unreal or real according to their own inclinations, but this is from the perspective of two types of persons, not from the perspective of the person engaged in conventional usage.
However, apprehension by virtue of the cognition's own form is indeed common to both.
Otherwise, how could suchness and its having the form of that object be established merely through the force of a subverting cognition and the movement of conceptualization regarding a false form?
Furthermore, the basis for apprehension is the same for both perception and other types of cognition.

The opponent, however, considers that which is grasped by verbal cognition to be ultimately real; therefore, this introduction of a sublation occurs at the point of that misconception. Thus, there is a twofold establishment of two cognitions: the apprehension that grasps the form of a jar as excluded from both [its own and other classes] is the "apprehension," while the cognition that has a form excluded from only one side is the "ascertainment" (*vyavasāya*).

When an object does not exist in reality, there occurs an apprehension due to the power of conceptual forms governed by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of experience; this is a superimposition (*āropaṇa*), and its object is said to be "superimposed. Furthermore, even as a positive entity (*vidhi*), it cannot be intended for cognition, because in conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) there is no contact with the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—due to the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*)—and because of the contradiction involved. Even in the case of a jar, which is excluded from both [homogeneous and heterogeneous classes], there is only the apprehension of the jar as excluded from the heterogeneous, and not the apprehension of the differences within the homogeneous class.
This is by virtue of its capacity.
Furthermore, the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) does not manifest apart from being the object of a cognitive act;
nor is even the unreal apprehended as "unreal" by that very same cognition.
This is according to the maxim: "Even those things which are not means of valid cognition appear as if they were means of valid cognition with respect to their own objects.

Since both [subject and object] are merely the playful manifestations of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that grasps them, they do not manifest as distinct entities. Therefore, there is no possibility for even a conceptualized portion of an entity (*bhāva*)—such as form (*rūpa*), existence (*sambhava*), or the denotable (*vācya*)—to exist at the very root;
hence, there is no hope for one who relies on the merciless blow of the momentary destruction (*kṣaṇa*) of the Nyāya school.

Even when the properties of a universal (*jāti*) are postulated in the meaning of a word characterized by the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), they remain restricted to the characteristics of oneness, eternity, permanence, and individual pervasiveness;
for they are based on non-difference and because there is no interruption [of the concept], and because the object is cognized through that [exclusion]. To explain:
When two things are perceived, there may arise some cognition that follows their difference; this, which has no basis in convention, is grounded in the proximity of the objects themselves.

Just as proximity is desired [as the cause] for the eyes and other [senses] regarding their effects, which are cognitions, even in the absence of a universal (*jāti*); or just as a universal follows [its instances] according to their divisions;
so too, first of all, there is the causal complex for the production of a cognition of non-difference, namely, having perceived one audible object, [one perceives] a second.

Furthermore, one who perceives another individual cow or any other distinct cow does not lack a cognition of difference, thinking, "This too is a cow; this too is a cow. Moreover, as this cognition increases through the observation of various individuals, it is traditionally taught that there is an increasing universal (*sāmānya*) due to the nature of this distinct cognition.

And there is non-difference among the circles of individual cows, because even when there is a distinction such as hornless (*khaṇḍa*) or horned (*muṇḍa*), there arises a cognition of an object that is non-distinct from all others of a different class.

The property of things themselves is such that, when a specific [quality] is perceived even from among those of the same class, there is the conventional usage of "perceiving difference. This is because there is no absolute non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) of the entire circle of cow-individuals; and because of the excellence of the collection of temporal moments, even eternity belongs to the category of the exclusion of heterogeneous things (*vijātīyāpoha*), since each instance is presented as a cognition excluded from others in its entirety.
The complete presence [of the property] in each individual instance is very firm, and its falsity depends upon a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*);

therefore, with respect to that, whatever has been cognized by this [means of knowledge] cannot be made otherwise. This is not a mere false conceptualization bound to a real entity, like the appearance in a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Even in the absence of that [external object], its arising would simply be like that of a memory; however, where the production of a determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) is constrained [by an object], there is indeed reality.

Even if the form (*ākāra*) is unreal, because it is excluded from what is other—despite the presence of exclusion—even when the external object exists, the "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) alone is the underlying continuity (*anugama*).
And that [object], though real, is so because of correspondence; though conceptual, it is so because it manifests within the conceptualizing intellect.
For a momentary cognition, being non-continuous, is incapable—like memory—of cognizing external objects or their impermanence.
For just as memory, although not itself past, remembers its own pastness, so too this [conceptual construction] is said to be "superimposed" (āropita).
And that object which is grasped through the appearance of a graspable form mounted upon conceptualization is called "superimposed.

For example, even in the absence of an external object, when fire is thought of for the sake of warmth—whether it be present or absent—the fire therein does not exist as excluded from both [the similar and the dissimilar], but it does exist as excluded from what is of a different class; such is the nature of conceptual thought.

That which is perceived through the power of formlessness is called "superimposed" (*āropita*), and it is also pervasive over what is non-existent. Furthermore, by the force of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*), there is likewise a failure to grasp the distinction between states; yet, because there is a perception of difference from what is heterogeneous, there is the capacity to grasp the difference from what is homogeneous.
By this, the following [objection] is refuted: "The common form is the object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and it cannot be unreal (*alīka*) while existing in such a manner."
For its conformity to space and time is not intrinsic,
because it is of the nature of a void;
nor is it conceptual, because it is non-momentary.
It is not superimposed, because it is not established elsewhere either.
If it is argued that unity alone is synthesized due to the non-apprehension of difference, we say no, because there is an absence of any real difference.
Alternatively, if it were an entity, its being conceptual would be contradictory;
for that which is ultimately non-existent must terminate in ultimate non-difference [from reality],
and it is impossible to perceive what is superimposed, as there would be no occasion for the superimposition of non-difference.

For one who has superimposed [the notion of] a sentient being upon that which is ultimately real, there follows the consequence of being devoid of the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), because of its non-conceptual nature;
for the grasping of such [a thing] is easily found even throughout the three worlds.
If it is argued, "In other cases as well, when a difference is perceived as ultimate, how can non-difference be superimposed?", then in that case, for whomsoever...
That which is necessarily superimposed upon a manifestation is precisely that which is not manifesting; it is not merely a matter of name, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For this very reason, the non-apprehension of a difference—whether it exists in a different locus or does not exist at all—is not conducive to the superimposition of non-difference.
Having understood the view of the author of the *Ṭīkā*, what indeed is this [objection] that has been raised against that position? (6)

What is called "superimposition" (*kilāropa*) is intended as a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of something upon another, based on the perception of a common property (*sādharmya*), such as the [superimposition] of silver upon mother-of-pearl;
therefore, this [notion] should be discarded by the young students dwelling in this wretched village.
There is much more that remains to be said. (7)
He spoke with the intention that, at the very least, some [result] will be obtained in the end—the fame of the author of the treatise.
Furthermore, [the objection] beginning with "Nor is Apoha established by logic, because of its absence" has also been refuted.
As for the alternative [position] regarding commonality (*sādhāraṇya*), it cannot be a dual nature, because that would involve a contradiction.
It is not its property (*dharmatva*), because that is not admitted;
for it is not admitted that "cowness" (*gotva*) is a property even of a non-entity (*abhāva*).
Nor is it its substratum (*dharmitva*), because of the lack of exclusivity (*anekāntāt*).
For even an individual (vyakti) possesses both presence and absence, and thus is not of the nature of negation alone;
therefore, there is no dissimilarity between those two [the universal and the individual] because such a thing is impossible.
If it were so [of the nature of negation] merely through the exclusion of what is other than that, then there would be no distinction from the probandum (sādhya).
Nor can there be co-referentiality between "exists" and "does not exist," because of their mutual contradiction and because [the latter] is established otherwise;
for that which exists cannot be the object of the cognition "it does not exist."

If it is argued that [the entity] must indeed exist by resorting to another mode, then what contradiction is there in establishing its positive nature (*vidhi*) by taking up that very distinction of modes, such that the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) would be established?
If it is asked, "Even if it has a positive form, what more is to be added by the word 'exists' (*asti*)?", then it is the same for its negative form: "What more is to be removed?
If it is argued that this is precisely why it is common to both cases, even so, it remains impossible to determine whether this [entity] consists of both or is the negation of both.

Therefore, whether it be the attainment of another attribute (*upādhi*) through "existence" and "non-existence," or the restriction of an attribute already attained, those two [terms] possess meaning.

This is equally true for the case of affirmation (*vidhi*). However, in the position that [the world] is unreal (*alīka*), since all particularities have been stilled, where could there be the prescription of another attribute or its restriction? Thus, this is a specific defect [of that view].
Consequently, the word "cow" culminates in denoting individuals qualified by the universal *gotva* (cowness).

However, because these individuals are scattered across different places and times, they are unable to fulfill the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) sought by the seeker; thus, the cognizer desires further specification.

And that desire of his regarding the cow Kālākṣī in the pen—which is characterized by such qualities as being "Dhanurghaṭodhnī" and "Mahāghaṇṭānandinī"—is restrained by various restrainers or enjoiners;
thus, there is no fault whatsoever in the case of a positive injunction.
So it is said.
That too is observed to be like the discharge of an arrow without a target;
for instance, O tree,
by the word "tree," only the affirmation of a tree is performed.

A positive injunction (*vidhi*) is, for example, as follows: when a negation is being performed by means of perception or by the nature of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), it is not possible [for that negation] to be connected with the words "exists" or "does not exist," because of the necessity of [the object] existing, or because of the necessity of its not existing. Likewise, is this word a positive injunction, [or is it] fit to be connected with these two words?
It is thus demonstrated.
In this way, a term common to both "existent" and "non-existent" has been demonstrated.

And that which is common to them—either as the exclusion of non-trees (*avṛkṣavyāvṛtta*) or as the positive affirmation of the object "tree"—is such an object [that constitutes] an external entity. (8)

Because there is no such designation by this [term] for that which is designated as either necessarily non-existent or necessarily existent through its exclusion from its own class (*sajātīya-vyāvṛtti*),
that referent of the word is common to both existence and non-existence, since it is observed in both. Furthermore,
it is common just as [the property of being] "heard" is common to both permanent and impermanent things because it is observed in both.

It has been stated that "knowability" (*prameyatva*) or "reality" (*vastutva*) is common [to both], just like that; however, it is not common to both because it consists of both existence and non-existence. Furthermore, any other conceptualization is fruitless, as it was intended otherwise;
for every verbal property (*dharma*) is indeed observed in those two kinds of properties.
This commonality is understood even by children; for instance,
just as there is a persisting cognition of the substratum amidst things characterized by appearance and disappearance,
so too is there a cognition of that substratum.
Knowledge would exist prior to the grasping of dharmas.
Thus is the view of Bhaṭṭa:

having observed a single substratum (dharmin) which is the locus of various attributes, when one [attribute] is affirmed, it appears as if possessing that [attribute], while remaining indifferent toward the others.
Just as the intellect constructs a threefold conventional usage— which lacks objective reality— consisting of a negation, that which is distinct from it, and that which depends upon others;
so too do those who have resorted to the basis of differentiation [construct] that very object of non-conceptualization in such a manner.
They run after worldly objects that have arisen from beginningless habitual tendencies.
The noble one, having attained various fruits or not yet attained them, is distinguished from this and that state,
as if his accumulations have been led away by various disturbances.
Therefore, those who rely on the distinction of views have failed to understand [the truth] and are thus frustrated.
Thus, the Master’s own essential tenet was stated at the very outset:
"The kind of cognition that is observed from words regarding things that have perished as well as those that have not perished is exactly the same for real objects;
this is not the case for cognitions of beauty and the like."
By the first half [of the verse], it was stated that the appearance of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is common to both existence and non-existence.

By the second half, it is shown that because the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)— the state of having the ultimate as its object— is absent, the proving property (*sādhanadharma*) lacks the quality of being common to both existence and non-existence.
In the case of the mind [cognizing] the ear and so forth, which possesses the property of the counter-example (*vipakṣadharmin*), this formal argument (*prayoga*) arises:
whatever cognition has an appearance that is common to both the presence and absence of a given object does not, in the ultimate sense, have that as its object.

For example, the appearance in a cognition of doubt; and the appearance in a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of sugar and so forth, which has an appearance common to both the presence and absence of the object consisting of sugar and so forth—[this is] by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Whatever cognition is, in the ultimate sense, directed toward a particular object, it conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that object;
just as auditory perception conforms to the presence and absence of the sweet sound of the *gāndhāra* note.

Furthermore, the appearance [of sugar] does not conform to the existence or non-existence of its own object characterized as sugar; for, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the appearance in the cognition of one who lacks sugar is seen to have that [sugar] as its object only by virtue of the relationship of causal origination (*tadutpatti*). If, however, [the appearance] were to occur even in the absence of that [object], then the appearance in the cognition of one whose ears are impaired would likewise [have an external object].

In ultimate reality, it would follow that [the cognition] has that as its object; in that case, it would also follow for the appearances of doubtful and erroneous cognitions. Yet, a proponent of valid cognition does not accept those two as being such [i.e., having external objects], because they lack the status of being objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Apart from this, no other cause can be postulated.

Just as the cognition of a cow cannot have another object [as its basis], so too it is not tenable; yet, while conforming to that cognition of a universal, how is it that the delineation of the form of blue and so forth is manifested within it? By whom was that produced?
Thus, whatever cognition does not have a certain appearance, it should not be designated as having that as its object.

For example, the cognition of a cow is not conventionally designated as having a horse as its object; likewise, a conceptual cognition (*kalpavijñāna*) has the appearance of color, shape, and the form of syllables, but it does not have as its object a universal (*sāmānya*)—as accepted by others—which is devoid of color, shape, and the form of syllables. For being the object of something is pervaded by the appearance of that thing; this is observed in the case of a visible form (*rūpa*), where the appearance of form is seen in relation to the object of form, and [likewise] in taste (*rasa*). (4)
Because of the qualification "tied with a cloth from the perspective of ultimate reality" (*paramārthataḥ*), it cannot be [said to be] merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*).

And the ultimate reality is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity, which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*) and appears directly to all worldly agents in their activities of rejection and acquisition.
The subject matter is now illuminated: "That which is capable of causal efficiency is alone ultimately real;
the other is declared to be conventionally real. These two are the particular and universal characteristics"—this is the meaning.
Therefore, this [objection] is irrelevant: "If the conceptualization of a cow has as its object only a horse, then its exclusivity (*asādhāraṇya*) would likewise apply to the external cow;

consequently, it would be characterized by the very property to be proven (*sādhyaviśiṣṭatva*). In that case, its exclusivity consists in the lack of expectation for specific qualities such as color and so forth.
For the generic term "cow" as cited does not require a specific qualification such as "horse" and so forth;

however, in the case of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), there is indeed a contradiction. For that which does not have a certain object as its domain cannot possibly require a restriction to its specific details.
Because it would follow that there would be a requirement for a restriction to a specific horse regarding the cognition of a cow;
and if you claim that its existence or non-existence is not demonstrated, then the fault is that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*).
For it has never been established for me that the conceptual construction of a cow does not demonstrate the actual form of a cow.
"And as for you, even now,
if there were another limiting condition (*upādhi*), [the reason] would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For there is no such rule that 'whatever does not demonstrate another limiting condition for something must not possess it either.'"
Furthermore, it has been stated: "How is the exclusion of its being non-cow (*agotva*) established?

It is conveyed by word and logical mark (*liṅga*), but not by a particular (*viśeṣa*), because [the word] functions as the very nature of the thing itself, and because other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and other words function in the same way. To explain:
When the single nature of an object is itself directly perceived,
what other entity could there be that is not seen and yet must be examined by means of valid cognitions?
A subject established through direct perception (*sahi-pratyakṣa*) is not a locus for a proof, because a means of proof (*sādhana*) is impossible therein.

For example, when "being a cognition" (*pratyayatva*) is the property to be proven, sound (*śabda*) is [not the locus], because it is already established by direct perception itself; since it is established in all its aspects, there is no other [aspect] that remains unestablished.

Or, if [the property] exists, it cannot have that as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); for it is not logical that what does not exist at certain times should be the intrinsic nature of something, since the conventional usage of distinction is based solely on that [existence]. Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of non-existence, as has been stated. Therefore, because perception determines the entirety of the intrinsic nature of the subject (*dharmin*), there is no room here for the cognition of another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Otherwise, it would be joined with another quality by means of a cause of error, just as the form of silver appears in mother-of-pearl due to the perception of a similarity in appearance.
If, even for one who has perceived all reality, other qualities were not superimposed by a cause of error that obstructs certainty—
just as the form of silver is [superimposed] upon mother-of-pearl— it would follow that those two forms would be perceived as identical and indistinguishable in the case of the mother-of-pearl.
Or, if there were no cognition [of it], then because of the impossibility of non-conceptualization through distinction, and because of the over-extension [of the consequence],
one who perceives the form of the mother-of-pearl perceives it as something specifically qualified; this is due to the deficiency of a determinative cognition (*niścaya-pratyaya*).

One thinks, "I perceive your universal as indeterminate," and from that arises the superimposition (*samāropa*) of silver. Likewise, even with respect to a similar object, because its difference has not been characterized at the time of its arising, there occurs a delusion of stability due to the superimposition of error. As many as are its extrinsic natures (*parabhāva*), so many are the superimpositions that arise according to their respective causes; therefore, these [cognitions] serve to exclude them.
Means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are effective [only] when they possess a result;

however, for those whose result is exclusion (*vyavaccheda*), there is no activity directed toward making known an aspect of an object already perceived, because that [aspect] has already been seen. Furthermore, it is impossible to perceive a portion of the result by means of a single part [of the object].
Therefore, every quality of a perceived entity is indeed perceived;
it is not "unsteady" due to error, and thus the means of proof proceeds.

When a single property (*dharma*) is ascertained through inference upon the apprehension of a real entity (*vastu*), the apprehension of all properties follows; this fault does not apply in the case of exclusion (*apoha*). Therefore, the logical mark (*liṅga*) is proclaimed to have exclusion as its object.
Otherwise, if the subject is already established, what further means of proof could there be for it?

Even when something is seen in some respect, that cognition which conceptualizes a general object has as its domain the exclusion of other factors (*apoha*) limited to that [aspect] alone, provided there is no superimposition (*asamāropa*) regarding other parts.
The object of a mind that has superimposed a certainty is subject to the relationship of the sublated and the sublator;
thus it is understood that its activity occurs upon the removal of that superimposition.
As many as are the superimpositions of parts, so many are the certainties regarding their exclusion;
and there are just as many words, for that reason they have distinct domains.
Otherwise, since a single object would be pervaded by one word,
and the cognition [of it] would have no other object, there would be synonymy.
Thus, having presented his own view, he has stated the subject for the sake of destroying the supreme delusion:
"For one who holds that the cognition of an object possessing various attributes is apprehensive of distinct things,
the factors that assist those various attributes are included within the apprehension of the self which is non-different from its powers."
What uncertainty could there be regarding the distinction between the two effects of the ego-sense, since both are related to the self? When one is made known, there is the apprehension of both.

Because the relationship of mutual assistance between the substrate (upādhi) and that which possesses it (tadvat)—which are essentially one—is apprehended, both are apprehended within a single cognition. Thus, when that [substratum] is apprehended as qualified by even a single attribute, there is the apprehension of all attributes, since the apprehension of the substrate is inseparable from the apprehension of those [attributes].
Otherwise, it would not be apprehended in that manner.
For there can be no helper of another that is not itself perceived;
nor, when the harmer is thus perceived, can there be a non-perception of that which is harmed, because that would entail the non-perception of the harmer as well.
Therefore, this same logical consequence applies even to the theory that [the universal] has external adjuncts (*arthāntaropādhi*).

If there is a distinction between the powers that assist the dharma, what is its [the dharma's] relation to them? If there is no assistance from them, then those [powers] would likewise be infinite regressions.
When a single beneficiary is to be apprehended, there are no other benefits besides that;
since it is seen, those which are unseen [in it] are [already] apprehended, and thus upon the apprehension of that, there is the apprehension of the whole.

By this [argument], if one were to accept a nature distinct from the relationship with limiting conditions (*upādhi*) characterized by ultimate dependence (*pāratantrya*), there would be a total collapse [of all cognition] through even a single means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or word (*śabda*) being employed. For when an entity exists, its state of being that [entity] is simply its existence;
and since the relationship of cause and effect is established through perception and non-perception, [the causal relation is self-evident].
Conceptual constructions, which have as their object only the reality of cause and effect,
display objects that are false in nature, as if they were composed of real things.

If [the cause] were distinct [from the effect], what would the production [of the effect] be? Or even the relation of cause and effect—if an entity were indeed separate from another, how could those two not remain either disjoined or conjoined?
By this, all [categories] such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) have been examined;
because they do not mutually benefit one another, such things cannot constitute a relationship.
Thus, this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) arises through a relationship based on an imagined state of benefactor and beneficiary;

for by what means could one perceive, even prior to depending upon an effect, an entity that partakes in the relation of cause and effect—though it is not yet conceptualized—such that this consequence would follow?
For this very reason it was said: "This fault follows as a consequence only by way of exclusion (*apoha*)."
Just as with the sun and so forth, when a planet whose nature is to benefit the entire world is apprehended, there would be an apprehension of the entire world. For this very reason, it is said:
"If, for the sake of removing error, something other [than the object itself] is desired to be apprehended."

It might be argued: "When a partless entity is grasped, what else could there be that is not grasped? It is simply not determined due to error. If this is so, then it is established that another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) has as its object the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of that [error]; and likewise, another [means of cognition] has as its object the exclusion of that [other].
Furthermore, since their activity occurs within a domain free from superimposition, how can that form which is not ascertained by their determinations be their object?

Now, it is established that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which functions for the purpose of removing error has the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropa-vyavaccheda*) as its result; thus, like that, another [means of cognition] also has the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) as its object, because it operates upon an object free from superimposition. Since there is no ascertainment regarding that which is not superimposed, it is established that the object of the exclusion of others is that in which there is an absence of superimposition.

But perception, by virtue of its established appearance, apprehends dependence and so forth, though it is devoid of intrinsic nature. Without effort, it thus establishes that which has removed the mass of faults inherent in its own nature;
for even when a particularity is apprehended by perception, that cognition which exists upon the determination of a specific feature is what is cognized.
Thus, this cause of conceptual cognition consists of habituation, proficiency, and the like, which possess degrees of intensity and so forth.
For example, regarding the body of a single woman, there arise three conceptualizations: a corpse, a mistress, and food, respectively, for an ascetic, a lustful man, and a dog.

Regarding such arguments presented by the author of the *Vārttika*, we do not even have the strength to write down the things he has prattled— utterances that, though intended with subtle and clever intellect, are like a snake whose venom does not spread, yet consist mostly of wide-spread hissing; for,
since they were composed by one who obtained his status through bowing to Maheśvara, they are not fit to be presented as a source of laughter.
If you claim there is another limiting condition (*upādhi*), then the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For there is no rule that whatever does not demonstrate another limiting condition for something must itself not belong to that thing.
But surely there is indeed such a rule?

For instance, that which does not cause the cognition of a property co-inherent with something else does not cause the cognition of its own nature, just as the conceptualized word for "cow" does not [cause the cognition of] a horse.

And likewise, those two [the word and the concept] do not [cognize] even the cow with respect to its blueness; thus, there is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Even when there is cognition of the substratum (*dharmin*), there may be cognition of some properties and non-cognition of others; this restriction would be due to a difference in assistance (*upakāra-bheda*).
Furthermore, a distinction in assistance would arise from a distinction in capacity;
however, this is not the case here, because it would lead to an infinite regress. Therefore, there is no distinction in capacity.

If there is no difference in the assistance [rendered], then there are only two possible courses: either awakening accompanied by all its conditions is itself awakening, or it is not; thus, the logical connection (*pratibandha*) is established.

This is poorly argued, because even when a distinction is postulated based on the conditions, the fact that something is cognizable by a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is likewise dependent upon the diversity of intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
Because that [power] also depends upon its own cause,
and because that [cause] is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), and because that [concomitance] is to be inferred from the effect;
as for the argument beginning with "because power is non-different," and so forth—

That [distinction] would be justified if it were dependent solely on the substratum (*dharmin*), or dependent solely on the cognition thereof, or dependent on the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for the cognition of that much, until the distinction of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is cognized; but this is not the case.

Let knowledge arise through whatever causal complex it may—does one accept or not accept that a substance which partakes in a relationship of benefactor and beneficiary (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*) based on two ultimate natures is actually perceived? Or is it not?

If that cognition has perceived [the object] in its entirety along with its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), then [you must] examine it closely: if, even in part, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is accepted as the object, then since the entity— which is established as the exclusion of what it is not— is determined by that cognition to have a nature capable of being assisted by non-ultimate limiting adjuncts, examine this skillfully.
To this extent:

when the consequence has been presented with respect to the cognition that apprehends [an object], you say, "I am merely touching the hair while leading away the head, because of the diversity of the causal complex. Therefore, why do you not perceive that cognition itself—along with all its adjuncts—is the nature of a thing capable of mutual assistance, existing in dependence upon one another?

The very nature of the object is rendered otherwise; this is the nature of cognition produced by that [means], and thus it determines the referent of that term as qualified by a single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). In the confidence of ultimate conceptualization, what else could this be than a mere ivory peg?

However, regarding the case where the object of another conceptualization is involved, it is quite evident that the aforementioned defects are not avoided and that the status of being a "productive cause" (kāraka-hetu) follows; thus, one who mocks in this manner is indeed laughable.

By this, [the argument] that even if there is a cognition of the substratum (dharmin) through its difference, the cognition of the difference among properties (dharmas) via words or logical marks should not also occur via the sense organs—such talk is rejected as being like twitching the buttocks when the ear is touched.
Because that which is [logically] entailed is accepted at a time when the causal complex for perceiving those respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is absent;
and because means of valid cognition possess diverse capacities,
since the capacity of a logical mark (*liṅga*) consists in the recollection of a well-established invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*).

Because the operation of a word is limited by convention (*samaya*), whereas a sense organ depends on the power of the object (*artha-śakti*)—and not because the object is merely connected—it is established by means of valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*);
otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This too is correct, as it does not deviate from the previous investigation.
Moreover, it is said that a word functions by excluding [others];

therefore, how could there be exclusion for you? Furthermore, how could a real entity be so characterized? Moreover, if it functions without exclusion, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it were admitted to function both there and elsewhere, the mention of its name would be useless; and if it were admitted to function and not to function [simultaneously], there would be a single injunction for two things. (2)
Otherwise, this statement would merely be a description of exclusion; therefore, the exclusion must necessarily be indicated by the word itself.

And that [exclusion] is non-different from it, while other properties of individuals and universals also exist; thus, there is the acceptance of what is restricted to that, the indication of the restricted, and the establishment of the meaning of the universal—having abandoned [the alternative], (3)
The further conceptualization of this [universal] is merely a stubborn adherence to what is useless, because it cannot be logically established according to such conceptualization.
It is certainly not that exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is not performed;
rather, it is the forms of universals (*jātirūpa*) that indicate the object of engagement (*pravṛttiviṣaya*).
"But is there not this much purpose for words, namely, the exclusion of difference? [The reply is:

"What is that? Is it not the case for you that a universal (*sāmānya*) is not distinct from another? A genus (*jāti*) is not capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and thus it is not the object of purposeful activity."
By that same reasoning, the objection regarding the lack of engagement [with the universal] has also been answered.

Similarly, there is an intervention in the case of the injunction; for if the two possessors of the universal (*jāti*) were the objects of engagement, then exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) would be the end of that [process]. Why is this not accepted? If it is argued that exclusion is not a means of proof because it is a non-entity (*avastu*), that is equal [to the case of the universal]; since it is a means of proof in that same way, there is no fault.

If this is argued, it is the same for that which possesses exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). For those who maintain the theory of exclusion, verbal cognition—which grasps a non-entity, arises with a variegated appearance, and determines its object as a causal factor—induces activity.
However, correspondence with a real entity occurs only when there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between that [cognition] and the production of the real entity.

If it is argued that otherwise there would be neither the production of a real object nor error, we say no; for that is not established because there is no determination of it as such. Furthermore, if it is argued that error lacks correspondence with a real object because we observe the error of a jewel in the luster of a jewel, we say no; for there is a deviation from that very point as already stated.
For the definition of error is a false appearance (*vitathapratibhāsa*); correspondence follows from its being invariably concomitant with that [false appearance], and not from the appearance itself.

Whether one accepts the apprehension of a universal (*jāti*) or the apprehension of an error, there is no engagement with that [universal]; what, then, is the use of it? For activity occurs through the manifestation of a cognition in the form of an object such as "blue" which is capable of action and is excluded from others.
Engagement with or withdrawal from other things arises appropriately based on what is presented by that [cognition], even without a universal.
Furthermore, because there is a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the thought "this is that" regarding objects that are distinct by nature.
Having observed various purposeful activities such as cognition and so forth, objects— even though they are distinct—
function together with linguistic expressions whose objects consist in the exclusion of what is other than them.
One should perform recognition by connecting [the past and present] even upon seeing this.

Even though there is difference, just as in the case of the eye and other [senses], the causal efficiency (arthakriyā) such as cognition occurs by its very nature; likewise, when one perceives that same causal efficiency in other objects which are excluded from what is not of that nature, there arises a false cognition (mithyājñāna) in which difference is conflated— due to the awakening of the latent impression (vāsanā) of one's own experience— consisting of the thought "this is that very thing," wherein the exclusion of others is not clearly distinguished.
Otherwise, the cognition would possess both difference and relation, like [the cognition of] a staff-bearer.
For by the perception of a single staff, it does not occur with respect to another that "this is that very same one"; rather, it occurs that "that is here."
But recognition is not like this—namely, "this is that very same thing"—for even one who perceives a single entity in multiple locations is not free from the association of difference.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction with such cognition because it occurs through the power of error (*vibhrama*), and that error is not absent due to the lack of a cause for it, [we reply: (3)

Those very entities, which perform that same function, are the cause by virtue of being, through the medium of experience, the natural cause of the delusive portion—the latent impression of conceptual construction.

For even in the case of mirages and the like, those two entities themselves—which produce an experience that serves as the cause for the cognition of a non-differentiated apprehension of water—are the cause of the illusion of water; though they are distinct, there is no other universal (*sāmānya*) whatsoever therein that is perceived in such a way.
Alternatively, if cognition apprehending a real object regarding an existent entity were not an error, then,
given that it is an error due to the superimposition of an unreal aspect, that very aspect must be its object;
for there is no superimposition of what is not an object.

And that superimposition, which consists in the apprehension of a universal as performing a single function, is a useless production; for conceptual constructions lack the capacity to apprehend the intrinsic nature of things as they actually exist, because they proceed from their own causes.

And their cause is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of ignorance, just as blurred vision is the cause of the illusion of hair-tufts. Thus, there exists this [superimposition] which arises from an internal affliction.
Arising from defects by its very nature, that [cognition] appears as if it were disciplined,
even though it disregards the perception of similarity and so forth, like the visual impairment known as *timira*.
Even for another [perceiver], that cognition does not arise from the universal alone;
for if it were known solely through that [universal], it would follow that the individual instances are never cognized.
If, however, the individuals—assisted by a single entity [the universal]—are the cause of cognition, [then they must be admitted as real].
Does that single object remove their diversity?
And because they are diverse, their status as the cause of a single cognition is not observed in them.

Alternatively, if production occurs when there is an absence of deficiency— that is, when there is the conjunction of those [causes]— then even if there are many [causes], they might produce a single cognition by depending upon one another.
Yet, even without those [auxiliaries], each [cause] would still produce the cognition individually.
Therefore, they lack that capacity even individually; thus, there is no grasping [of them] by the intellect.
Now, just as in the case of blue and other [colors], visual consciousness arises even when one is absent, and thus they do not lack capacity even in their aggregate, so it is here as well. (10)

It is not the case that because [the color] exists in the dyed cloth (*kāṣāya*), it lacks capacity in all circumstances; for this is not so, since the individual capacity of blue and other colors is observed separately in visual consciousness.
While the establishment of power may exist in an aggregate, it is by no means the same in the case of a manifestation.

For individual instances (vyakti) are not observed to have the power to produce a recurring cognition when devoid of a universal (sāmānya); therefore, since they are incapable in that regard, they would not be apprehended by it. If that [universal] is capable even in dependence on any one of them, it is not [capable] alone.
Why then do they not produce a single cognition as well?

Since, due to their previous association with cooperative causes, they have obtained a universal as something to be assisted—just like those [cognitions] that require another universal—what obstruction is there for them to produce a single cognition? For, produced without that [single cognition], they would be false, as they would lack their own object.

Thus, having raised the suspicion of falsity (2), the mental disputes regarding the cognitions of the Buddha have already been addressed. Likewise, there is no cognition of a subject that possesses a manifold nature through the sense-faculties in every respect;
rather, the object of the sense-faculties is a form that is self-cognizable and inexpressible.

For one who has turned away from everything, the very process of turning away from this or that [object] constitutes the manifold nature of the subject, its diversity being inferred from the diversity of those [objects].
Those imagined distinctions of form are not the object of a non-conceptual mind that is variegated and occasional, appearing as diverse manifestations.
Even though there exists whiteness and so forth, just as it is within the range of the senses,
that [object] is not denoted by words because of the difference in form between the two cognitions.
Even if the objects of the cognitions are one and the same, if [the difference] were due to their having different substrates;
Now, as for the consideration of the ear and the other [senses], why is it that they have distinct objects?
Since the mutual bases of cognitions regarding that single object have arisen as distinct,
how can there be a single form appearing with diverse aspects?

If the appearance of variegated and non-variegated forms belongs respectively to conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions based upon the eye, its marks, and sound, then how can they have the same object in the ultimate sense? Alternatively, while one [the non-conceptual] has the ultimate as its object, the other [the conceptual]—due to causes such as ignorance and other secondary conditions—is like that which, through the power of cataracts, jaundice, and so forth, produces the appearance of yellow and the like toward what is white. From all these [perspectives], [their identity is untenable].
When the partless (*akhaṇḍa*) entity has ceased,

another [cognition] arises which has a non-ultimate object as its domain; this is caused by the difference in causes, because it produces a conceptual appearance that is incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), having acquired a state of being a subject and a predicate (*dharmadharmibhāva*) that is restricted to the exclusion of others and serves as the cause for the intended causal efficiency.
And when it is said, "Let it be established by the difference in expression," [the consequence] "moistening" (kleda) is attached [to the argument].
This is because there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to the two appearances—variegated and non-variegated—which are mutually contradictory yet have the same blue object;

for in the case of a variegated perception, that which shines as blue is not the very same [blue] for another person, such that those two would have identity of object through that very form, nor is there contradiction through that [identity].

If it is argued that there is no single object of cognition where there is contradiction, because contradiction exists through the form of one property while the single objecthood exists through the form of the mere individual (piṇḍa) as blue—then [we reply]: here too, contradiction exists through the form of another property, while the single objecthood exists through the form of the mere individual such as "cowness" (*gotva*); therefore, if you negate only that much, your reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
In the previous case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

For we do not admit that at the time of verbal or inferential conceptualization, all specific properties (*dharmaviśeṣa*), such as the restriction of place and time, actually become objects of cognition.

For even if you say that the unmanifest is of the nature of a failure of maintenance (*nirvāha-bhraṃśa*), you still cannot escape the consequence of following after the object of cognition (*prameya*). Here, variety (*citrata*) is intended as the state of being a property of the subject (*dharmidharmatā*); how then can that [variety] be non-exclusive (*anekānta*)?

If there were a non-conceptual [cognition] of those two blue [aspects] by means of two blue [objects], then the white [object] would be established as capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-samartha*), [despite] the appearances of the two blues.
How can conceptual cognitions, together with their determinate appearances, share a single object— like what is seen by the left and right eyes—
even though blue is perceived as both clear and unclear depending on its proximity or distance? In that regard,
the conceptual cognition perceives [the object] as distant in terms of space and time, whereas the non-conceptual cognition perceives it as proximate in terms of space and so forth.
It is not logical for [an object] to be both manifest and unmanifest through distinctions such as distance and proximity;
if it is argued that this is due to a difference in illumination, then [the same would apply] to its being covered or uncovered.
Whether it be a perception or a non-perception, they are equal; there is no subtle distinction whatsoever for him. Therefore, if a difference is perceived, it is due to a dim light.

If the external object were a single unity, how could there be a distinction between the visible and the invisible? If it were a plurality composed of distinct atoms, how could there be a distinction between the visible and the invisible? If you argue that the distinction in cognition arises from a difference in the clarity or dullness of the appearance, [then...]
When one thing is distinct, how can there be an appearance of something non-distinct through that distinction?
Even that light is faint; why is it not obscured here? This attenuation of light exists elsewhere as well, yet there is no lack of intensity.
And if that light were very close, it would be clearly and most distinctly perceived;
even in that case, if another form were to arise depending on the unseen (adṛṣṭa)?
Because they would mutually obstruct one another, their light would be thwarted;
consequently, only one at a time would be seen there, whereas if there were no such obstruction, all would be seen simultaneously.
If one were to see a form, whether clearly or unclearly, by means of a single [sense organ] that prevents what is unseen,
then what does that which is seen accomplish for one for whom neither benefit nor harm exists?

Whether the cause be unseen or seen, it must be postulated; for if the external object were a single unity, the proficiency with which it appears clearly or obscurely would be lost. It follows that the cognition itself must possess a determinate form at the appropriate time; otherwise, [the distinction between clear and obscure would be impossible]. (10)
For those who maintain that the determination of victory and defeat depends on external factors, the situation would be reversed:
it could be asserted that victory, by the power of unseen destiny (*adṛṣṭa*), is transformed into defeat, and defeat likewise into victory.
Therefore, consciousness arises according to its causes, based upon the object.
The remaining [doctrines], which are the fallacies of poor intellect, maintain a distinction based on mere appearances.
As for the objection: "Is there not, indeed, a distinction between clear and unclear appearances precisely regarding the subject (*dharmin*)?

For in whatever way properties (*dharmas*) appear, in that same way there is the conventional usage of the appearance of a clear object," and so forth—it has been stated more than once that appearance as subject and property is an unclear appearance because it is a conceptual construction due to the non-proximity [of the object] in terms of space and time, since its object is superimposed; thus, in the ultimate sense, it does not have that [external object] as its domain.
It is not accepted [as ultimate];
however, since the conventional [nature] is indeed proclaimed by the world, there is therefore the application of reflective consideration (*parāmarśa*).
Even the consensus of those who perceive reality has as its object blue that is excluded from what is not of that form by means of a coarse conceptualization;
it has as its domain multiple blues excluded from their own kind by means of an intermediate conceptualization.

Descriptions such as "being a real entity" and so forth—which are based solely on activity—are applied to that very blue [object] when they touch upon other intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*); through these [descriptions], there is also no sublation [of the perception], because the word and the logical mark function by way of recollecting the previously grasped relationship.

The cognition characterized as a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) has either an imperceptible object through an internal connection, or it has a perceptible object because it excludes what is present before one; yet even for these two, there is no identity of object in reality. If one accepts that this is a conventional cognition, then where is the contradiction?

Since the entire cycle of adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) has been cast into the belly of the non-perception of sublation, even Indra himself would not be able to proclaim "inconclusiveness due to doubt" by means of that [conceit].
Cognition, while bearing a single object, is observed to exhibit a variety of appearances— such as sharp, dull, or turbid— according to the differences among the sense faculties.
Since the object has an undifferentiated nature, the mind would be of a single form;
if [you argue] that all [cognition] is of the form of that object because of the object itself, then it lacks the appearance of that [object].
For that [cognition], which arises based on an object but does not assume its form,
there may nonetheless be a distinction from another [object] in respect to some of its aspects.
For then, although the son is of the same nature as his father by depending upon him,
he nevertheless maintains a distinction from his father in some respect or other.
Those with dull vision perceive a circle of light from a lamp or similar source, appearing like the eye of a peacock's feather and radiant with blue and red hues.
If that [cognition] were of an external form, what would be the objection to one with clear vision?
And how could a seer of reality, seeing that [external object], have impaired faculties?
When his eye, which is beyond the reach of the senses, has been purified of darkness and clearly perceives an object visible to other eyes, how could that same object again be unclear to him?

It is understood that, apart from the mental attention directed toward light and the eye, there is the capacity of one [specific factor] as the cause; therefore, how could anything other than that be the cause, or how could that which is not a cause be the object?
Thus, because there is no positive or negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) between the apprehension of another limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and its possessor (*tadvat*),
how could a difference in manifestation (*pratibhāsa-bheda*) occur even through that [adjunct], given the existence of a distinct cognition of the limiting adjuncts from the property itself?
Objects are the cause of such a cognition precisely by virtue of being properties of the real thing (*vastu-dharmatayā*).
Even when there is difference, wherever that cognition exists, it apprehends those things in such a manner.

The same applies to cognitions: when there is a distinction [between objects], yet a reflective awareness of non-difference occurs, this is not a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of a single entity, but rather of the non-separation of their effects.
Therefore, because [the capacity] exists in things, verbal testimony (śruti) is based upon them;
even though its state consists in the exclusion of external capacities, that verbal testimony [remains] directed toward them.
It is bound to the conceptual reflections that are based upon those [particulars];
therefore, because it is established in the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), the word is said to effect the exclusion of others.
The first half of the verse beginning with “*bāhyaśakti*” is the aphorism (*sūtra*) for the sublation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The second half, beginning with “*vikalpapratibimbeṣu*,” has the following meaning: because conventional activity proceeds by unifying the two objects—the manifest (*prakāśya*) and the object of conceptualization (*dṛśyavikalpa*)—it serves as the cause for linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) and so forth.
“That reflection of an object which appears in cognition as if it were distinct [from the cognition itself]... [is the definition of the object of conceptualization].
Even that [cognition] derived from words does not have the object as its essence; it is an illusion arising from latent predispositions (vāsanā).
When that [universal] is denoted, only one part—the object—is understood through the words;
and since that [object] is not apprehended, the act of establishing a convention for its sake would be useless.
It is said that a word expresses a portion of the object; in this regard, it is called "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha).

That mental image (ākāra) does not exist in the external object; how then can a word, by expressing that [image], be said to participate in the object? Furthermore, that [word] which possesses positive concomitance must have its effect [concomitance] with an object that likewise possesses positive concomitance.
Because cognition is non-differentiated,
that which is produced by the repeated practice of perception functions otherwise through the apprehension of a superimposition of that form;
thus, the statement that "the meaning of a word is that very object" is not contradicted.

Thus, by virtue of subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*), even though there is a contradiction in the exclusion of what is not that form (*atadrūpavyāvṛtti*), the meaning of a word is called *apoha*.

And that [apoha] appears as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) of the positive injunction (*vidhi*) immediately after the cognition of the injunction, because worldly activity proceeds through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*).
And as for how it delimits that, and so forth:
"In order to establish a meaning in a particular place, a word is employed by turning the mind away from something else, because of the determination of that specific object."
Otherwise, the application [of the term] would be useless; this applies even to words such as "that which is to be known" (tajjñeya) and so forth.

In those things brought forward in common usage, there is some form of exclusion; for that which is excluded from something else is what is to be negated. When there is a difference between them, among those things being differentiated, there appears a common form.
And this very [nature] of that entity is understood through the exclusion of others.
It is said that a "portion" is something that has no form whatsoever;
nevertheless, through words directed toward that [portion], the exclusion of others is understood.
In that regard, no one is understood to be superior or distinct from another;
nor does the word "mutual non-existence" (anyonyābhāva) itself effect such a duality.

"The perception of the formless as possessing form is a derangement of the intellect"—thus it has been clearly stated that apoha is merely exclusion (*vyāvṛttimātra*). Subsequently, the word-meaning is cognized;
that it "is cognized" was indeed correctly said.
First, the primary meaning is conveyed by words whose feet are friends; therein,
exclusion (apoha) is understood as a subordinate quality.

The referent is one from the perspective of superimposition, another from the perspective of appearance, or it may be established as something to be expressed; yet in reality, there is nothing at all.

Intending to point out his own lack of understanding regarding this much that was intended to be said, he says: "Indeed, the nature of a cow is described as being empty of color, function, syllable, and form."

When this much was intended to be said, [the opponent], pointing out the deficiency of his own understanding, says: "Even as for the statement beginning with 'of those things that are absolutely dissimilar,' etc., that too is inconclusive due to doubt; for such a conventional usage can be established even by a positive property (*vidhi*) of that kind. To explain: this conventional usage is not without a cause, nor does it have multiple causes, nor does it have a single cause that is not connected to multiple [things], because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)."

Furthermore, that which remains as the single cause for the manifold cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), and so forth—that too is described as "cowness" (*gotva*) devoid of color, shape, and the form of syllables;
[it is] devoid of color, shape, and the form of syllables. (3)
