(2) Regarding the commonality (*sāmānya*) intended by the majority: even for a commoner who has heard the account of the equal truth regarding whether the root has been washed or not washed, no distinction is perceived; for what indeed is this "exclusion" (*apoha*), which is a non-existence (*abhāva*) devoid of all color, shape, syllables, and forms, or is it the universal (*sāmānya*) that is excluded from what is not of that nature?

When it is stated that "the meaning of the word *adhyavasāya* (ascertainment) is a specific cognition characterized by the conceptualization of forms (*ākāra*), and it is the cause of all purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*)," one might ask: what is this *adhyavasāya*? Is it the appearance of a non-existent thing as a real entity, or is it [the appearance] as having the nature of a state [of consciousness], and is it therefore distinct from that [consciousness]?

Whether it be the grasping of a sign (*dāgraha*) or its arising from the latent impressions of things (*vastuvāsanā*), this expansion of irrelevant connections—though not the primary intended meaning—is as follows:

its validity (*pramāṇa*) consists in its similarity to the object (*arthasārūpya*), because the cognition of the object is established by virtue of that [similarity]; for conventional activity proceeds by unifying the perceived (*dṛśya*) and the conceptualized (*vikalpya*) objects. Furthermore, the establishment of the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) here is just as in the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), according to such statements; thus, there is the apprehension of specific qualities distinguished from the blue form.
In the established position that the apprehension of that [object] consists merely in the form of blue— which is excluded from what does not have that nature—
there is no similarity to the object, because such [similarity] is absent.
For what indeed could be the commonality between that which is real in the ultimate sense and that which is false in nature? Thus, where would the unification of molasses and milk be of any use?

For once its falsity has been established by a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*), why should one first superimpose it and then engage in such deliberation? Furthermore, the remaining fault lies solely in the conceit [of the opponent], as this has already been resolved through the consideration of the perception of silver.

If it were silver, what would be said? ... By the establishing [cognition], the existence of the object of the injunction must be established through another means of cognition; by the subverting [cognition], there is the negation of what is suspected or superimposed. Regarding the negation of place and so forth, it is well known that if something is restricted by place and time, then if it exists, it is negated.
It is not as it appears, nor is it as it exists; nevertheless, it is not negated.

As for the argument that, having introduced the point that activity proceeds from the similarity [of the object] to cognition (*jñānasārūpya*), it is established that one acts toward that which has already manifested— this merely proves what is already proven; for the similarity of cognition is held to be established by inference (*anumāna*),
and since that [similarity] exists, its status as being included within the non-mediated form of cognition is also established by inference.
Because it is included within the reflective awareness of the subjective aspect that is the locus of the ego, it is externalized and denoted by the manifested word.
If [you argue] that its occurrence with respect to the object is due to error because of similarity [between the cognition and the object], that would not be the case at all times;
furthermore, there is no spatial error in the cognition, since the arising of consciousness is uniform.
For a cognition of such a kind, since the intellect does not otherwise proceed toward that [external object],
it lacks validity either with respect to the appearance of an external object or with respect to its means.

...the state [of cognition] which has forms external to its own nature, the designation of "otherness," and the nature of being non-manifest; and because the ego is not of the nature of light, and because of the very existence of the blue object, it is thus stated that the intellect, whose object is the exclusion of that form, is perceived by its own cause through a direct observation—just as silver is [perceived] in mother-of-pearl; therefore, this [objection] is also refuted.

[Objection: "In that case, let [the cognition] direct [the person] toward its own manifest form; for one who has directed [their effort] toward that very thing obtains an object similar to it, just as one who has directed [their effort] toward the luster of a gem obtains the gem itself. [Response:
No, because there is no engagement with something that lacks the capacity for the intended purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
(4) There is no possibility of the occurrence of the form of conceptual construction externally, because that [external object] does not come into contact with it; furthermore,
the superimposition of externality occurs upon the form while its own nature is manifesting, since there is no opportunity for the superimposition of what is not its own nature.

"But in the case of the light [of a jewel], one who seeks the jewel proceeds toward it with the cognition of a jewel, and not with the cognition of that [light] itself"; thus the example is also fallacious. Having communicated such principles of reasoning, it was said: "Between one who runs toward the light of a jewel and one who runs toward the light of a lamp, both having the cognition of a jewel, although there is no difference in their being false cognitions, there is a difference with respect to purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)."
Just so, even though inference and its fallacy may lack correspondence with reality,
their status as valid cognition or its semblance is well-established by virtue of their conformity to purposeful action.

If it is argued that cognition appears in the form of blue because it arises as the manifestation of "this is indeed blue," being distracted by the aspect of the grasper and appearing as something external to conceptualization—[then the following applies]: the object of the blue and the non-blue is blue; [yet] cognition appears as having the form of blue.
"Other than those two, it is through inference... for the object of conceptualization is [located] in the subject (dharmin).
And that form which is self-awareness (*saṃvedana*) is not the cognition of that [external object]; this is not established [otherwise].
Having reached all these distinctions through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)."

Therefore, the claim that there is an external object established [by cognition] and that cognition possesses a form (*sākāra*) is merely the childish greed of those whose hearts are tormented by others; it is a mockery. Regarding the knowledge of the production of the manifest and unmanifest, blue is not non-cognition, nor is it a means consisting in the linguistic usage of a nature characterized by activity. That [blue], as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), appears as something external to the object of measurement (*meyabāhyatā*), being of the nature of cognition yet not permeated by the sense of "I" (*anahaṃkāra-kalita*). This is not the case in inference. It is characterized by the definition of the very first authoritative statement (*prāmāṇika-vacana*)... when [the object] is perceived.
The reason is that she remains delighted in the lotus-forest of the two worlds; this is not the cause of her sovereignty,
for even now she stays outside the ocean of her female elephant's mind.
Like a fire in a forest, [the nature of] the tree of the foolish is to be grasped... Furthermore, it was asked:
"Now, what is this so-called non-cow?"
Is the self of a single particular (svalakṣaṇa) of a cow something distinct from it, or is it devoid of the properties belonging to it?
In the first case, only Bāhuleya would possess the nature of a cow, while Śābaleya would be silent [on that point].

In the second case, however, that which is devoid of those properties would be excluded, and that which possesses them would be the cow; and regarding this, we have no dispute. Even if one argues thus, it would always be shown by means of its exclusion (apoha).

Cognition is non-different because it is the cause of a single unifying reflection (*pratyavamarśa*); likewise, individual instances are also non-different by virtue of being the cause of that single cognition.
This is for the sake of a single unifying reflection, in the accomplishment of a single purpose such as knowledge and so forth.
Even though there is a difference [between individuals], some are determined by their very nature, like the sense faculties and so forth.

Therefore, while you [the opponent] maintain that the entire mandala here is always perceived as an uninterrupted continuity, by which one does not see the ground, and while the non-existent [entities] proceed as mere measures, colors, shapes, and letters—[one who], failing to perceive even the single unifying cognition (*ekaparāmarśa*) produced by the mandala, understands [the object] through color and shape as distinct from those properties—it would follow that this is so. Even regarding the particular (*viśeṣa*), there is nothing that is not manifested; for linguistic usage proceeds by means of the very same [form]. Thus, if [you claim] that "form" (*rūpa*) exists in the state of individual manifestation (*vyaktitva*).

In that case, even a universal would be denotative of forms such as blue and so forth. It might be so because of the usage of "one," provided that others are treated as one with respect to something else; for if it were to treat others as one, then there would be a contradiction with the exclusion of what is of the same class as a deficiency of cognition. Furthermore, what is meant by "individuality" (*vyaktitva*)? Is it by way of being a speaker (*bhāṣakatva*)? (16)
Whatever is perceived by this [cognition], that alone is to be treated as a unity by it; thus, there is a powerful engagement.

Regarding the many universals, [the notion] "this is the denotative power here" is clearly established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), thereby distinguishing the cognition.
The unerring function of the intellect always exists in both primary and metaphorical [applications];
likewise, there is even a worldly convention regarding a lion and a young brahmin.

Where a word, even if its meaning is unreal, has been applied by people through conventional usage, that is its primary sense; elsewhere it is secondary (gauṇa), its application faltering because of its similarity to that primary sense.

People might apply the name "non-existence" even to that which exists, or they might do so according to their own conceptualization; or they might apply the Vedic revelation to Pradhāna and other such principles because of its incapacity [to produce effects].

Furthermore, that pervasive consciousness which appears as the manifestation of the word and the individual entity is described as "cowness" (gotva), for it is devoid of the forms of color, shape, and syllables.
If it were a genus (*jāti*), then even a single tree in a grove would be called a "garland" (*mālā*), just like a single tree [is called a "tree"].
If there is a plurality of garlands, how could that word apply to a genus, given that a genus is not itself plural?

Furthermore, that which is intended as "largeness" and so forth in a garland and the like is not figurative, because it is apprehended by a cognition that is indistinguishable from that of the primary object.
This lack of dependence on any other cause is equal in you to those things considered primary;
what other cause does the word "category" (padārtha) regard besides this group of six?
Whatever is established through conventional usage in a certain way, and whatever else is spoken of in that same way due to its similarity to it—
whether primary or secondary— is designated as "non-existence" with respect to entities by way of metaphorical transfer.

Conventional usage follows linguistic convention, and that [convention] is established according to the speaker's intention for the sake of practical communication, just like the names of meters and parts of words.
It arises based solely upon the formative impressions of conceptual construction.
Because it arises directly from an external cause and serves as the basis for that cause, it is the "obstructor of the cause.
Whether it be the word "awakening" (*bodhi*) or the awakening itself, it would cause [the object] to be known;
even in the absence of that [object], it would function without dependence, like a name, even when [the object] is concealed.
Out of fear, I desire to utter that [reality] which is dependent solely upon those [categories],
because one perceives its abiding state within that very consciousness of "mere-ness" (mātratā).
This is the convention, established from time immemorial, which has set aside the power of words.
The word "avyaya" (indeclinable) applies to that which initiates [an action], not to the object, but rather to the cognition.

But that relation of his [the word] to the object is something additional to its denotative capacity; it is not a property of another [the object], because it is by people that it is recognized as the cause of comprehension.
Even though it is an instrument, the action is minimal in its effect and does not reside in both [agent and object];
for since cognition lacks that duality, its cause is established therein.

How could there not be a distinction for one who does not act [based on] the cognition of the opposite of that? If all cognitions were cognitions of objects, then error would be cognized by cognition itself.
Everything indeed would be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) because it relies upon its own nature and so forth;
indirectness (parokṣatā) would be a means of valid cognition, being distinguished by the difference in its cause.
Furthermore, it is authoritative because its own utterance by the speakers brings about the comprehension of the intended meaning,
provided that the expressive word possesses independence.

There is no lack of independence when multiple cognitions have a single object produced by desire and so forth; for a single object is known by both consciousness (*vijñāna*) and cognition (*jñāna*), which are dependent upon their respective sense faculties.

Therefore, there is nothing else that serves as the cause for that [cognition], nor is there any means of cognizing that object itself; rather, the cognition of the substratum of the object is implied by the power of the relationship between the object and its [perceptual] basis.
In that regard, this confusion regarding what is not elsewhere has been brought about by others;
even in the absence of that [confusion], that which arises is in consideration of the questioner's statement.
[6] For what reason could one conceive [the thought], "Let there be no [arising]," or "The effect is empty"? [From the *Udayanirākaraṇa* composed by the Buddhist Nyāya master Śrī Ratnakīrti.]
